title: Digital Divide and Educational Inequality in Asia: A Cross-Country Secondary Data Analysis of Connectivity, Access, and Student Achievement
affiliations: and National University– Manila

detail.title: Digital Divide and Educational Inequality in Asia: A Cross-Country Secondary Data Analysis of Connectivity, Access, and Student Achievement

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study adhered to ethical standards for secondary data research. All data used in the analysis were obtained from publicly available and reputable institutional sources, including the World Bank, OECD PISA, and the International Telecommunication Union(ITU). The datasets are aggregated at the country level and do not contain personally identifiable information. As such, the study posed no risk to human participants and did not require formal ethical approval. Proper citation and acknowledgment of all data sources were maintained to ensure transparency, integrity, and responsible use of data.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Research, Innovation, and Strategies for Education (RISE), volume 3, issue 4, 2026[10.70148/rise.v3i4.9]

detail.abstract: The increasing reliance on digital technologies in education has intensified concerns regarding unequal access to digital resources across countries, particularly in developing regions. While digital connectivity has the potential to enhance learning opportunities, disparities in internet access and technological infrastructure may contribute to unequal educational outcomes. This study examines the relationship between the digital divide and educational inequality in Asia through a crosscountry secondary data analysis of connectivity, access, and student achievement. Using publicly available datasets from the World Bank, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the study analyzes key indicators of internet access, digital infrastructure, student achievement, and educational inequality across selected Asian countries. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multiple regression models were employed to examine structural associations among variables. The results indicate that internet access is positively associated with student achievement and negatively associated with educational inequality. Digital infrastructure also demonstrates positive associations with educational performance and lower levels of inequality. In contrast, rural population is negatively associated with student achievement and positively associated with educational inequality. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of digital connectivity and technological capacity in shaping both the quality and equity dimensions of education systems across diverse national contexts.

title: Strategic Format Choice Under Mandatory Machine-Readable Disclosure: Evidence and Theory from Hospital Price Transparency
affiliations: and

detail.title: Strategic Format Choice Under Mandatory Machine-Readable Disclosure: Evidence and Theory from Hospital Price Transparency
detail.abstract: Every United States hospital must disclose its negotiated prices in a common, machine-readable schema, yet federal auditors find over a third of sampled hospitals noncompliant and cannot confirm the files' usability. This paper models a choice the schema leaves open: report a negotiated rate as a plain dollar figure or as a percentage or algorithm with statistics summarizing its variation. A game-theoretic model shows the optimal format follows a single complexity threshold, its rent disciplined by the dispersion statistics required alongside it. When file production is delegated to a shared compliance platform, whether a hospital's strategic behavior remains visible in its disclosure depends on the platform, a joint product of vendor design and client sorting, not the hospital alone. Two collection waves over a national earlyadopter sample (195 and 299 hospitals) show both patterns: vendor and corporate platforms account for 75.4 and 86.3 percent of the waves by headcount, several show near-zero crosshospital dispersion, one corporate template withholds dollars for two thirds of its rates across 92 facilities, and one vendor's template reveals real hospital-specific complexity while codisclosing dollars. The paper contributes a mandatory-disclosure model whose only strategic margin is format, a boundary condition under which a shared platform's design determines whether the firm-level mechanism remains observable, a welfare analysis showing equilibrium format choice is socially excessively opaque, with a closed-form corrective penalty, and exploratory early-adopter evidence quantifying how much of a live mandate's observed variation is a property of the disclosure software rather than of the regulated entity.

title: Agentic AI and Autonomous Decision-making Systems: Architectures, Trust, Accountability, and Governance for Responsible Machine Autonomy

detail.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous Decision-making Systems: Architectures, Trust, Accountability, and Governance for Responsible Machine Autonomy
detail.abstract: Agentic AI is ushering in a new era of autonomous decision-making and action, moving beyond prediction, classification, and recommendation to digital systems that can plan, reason, act on the digital environment, and execute actions on their own (Kolt, 2025; Raza et al., 2026). This article aims to explore this shift through a conceptual synthesis of the research literature and a structured review of key conceptual ideas, focusing on agent architectures, autonomous decision processes, human-AI interaction, explainability and accountability, privacy, cyber security and governance trends, among others, published over the last 6 years (2021-2026). Five main findings are identified as a result of the synthesis. Agentic AI is a vast addition to the existing AI landscape because agents are able to break down goals into a series of steps, instead of just recommendations (Kolt, 2025; Raza et al., 2026). Second, the performance of autonomous decisions is not only dependent upon the intelligence of the model, but also on the ability to integrate reliable data, maintain persistent memory, plan, use external tools, interact with the environment and obtain feedback. Third, greater autonomy brings novel accountability and responsibility gaps as decision-making power can be spread among human operators, AI agents, data sources, models and technological infrastructures (Santoni de Sio & Mecacci, 2021). Fourth, humans are still needed, especially in a high-impact or consequential decision space (Popa & Rothkrantz, 2021; Alon-Barkat & Busuioc, 2023). Fifth, the trustworthiness, the explainability, the privacy, the security and the governance of the system should be part of the agent architectures in their design, not an afterthought as a post-deployment control (Walmsley, 2021). The results thus show an inherent contradiction in the shape of the greater the autonomy, the more accountability mechanisms are required. The responsible and autonomous approach to decision-making should not aim for full dehumanization of the decision-making process, but should be based on a model of controlled autonomy in which agents make autonomous decisions within specific boundaries and escalation mechanisms, auditability, transparency and human accountability are retained (Alon-Barkat & Busuioc, 2023; Santoni de Sio & Mecacci, 2021). The solution offers a starting point for adopting agentic AI and maintaining operational independence while adhering to responsible governance principles.

title: The Enterprise AI Culture Playbook
affiliations: The Digital Economist

detail.title: The Enterprise AI Culture Playbook
detail.abstract:
Eighty-eight percent of organizations now use AI. Yet only 6 percent can demonstrate measurable financial returns from their investments.
Why are so many companies investing in AI while so few are creating value?
The Enterprise AI Culture Playbook answers that question with a research-backed framework built for CEOs, board directors, and executive leaders navigating enterprise transformation. Drawing on findings from McKinsey, Boston Consulting Group, Harvard Business Review, PwC, Prosci, WRITER, and Informatica, Sandy Carter reveals the three pillars that consistently separate AI leaders from AI laggards: Change Management, Data Foundation, and Business Outcome Discipline.
Through real-world examples from Qualcomm, JPMorgan Chase, and Walmart, the playbook demonstrates how organizations can move beyond experimentation and build the culture, governance, and operating discipline required to scale AI successfully.
The paper also introduces AI Hollowing, a new organizational risk in which companies cut institutional knowledge in pursuit of AI efficiency, weakening their ability to realize AI value in the process.
The next phase of AI competition will not be won by organizations with the most advanced models. It will be won by organizations that master the 70 percent of transformation that technology alone cannot solve.
The question is no longer whether your company is investing in AI.
The question is whether it will join the 6 percent who win.

title: AI Alignment with Human Preferences
affiliations: The Digital Economist

detail.title: AI Alignment with Human Preferences
detail.abstract:
AI Alignment with Human Preferences examines how the rapid advancement of generative AI and large language models has intensified the need to align AI systems with human values, intentions, and societal expectations. Written by Manas Talukdar, the paper surveys the evolving landscape of AI alignment research, tracing both the technical foundations of alignment methodologies and the ethical, governance, and operational challenges associated with integrating human preferences into AI systems. Drawing from academic literature and industry practice, it explores key approaches including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), direct preference optimization (DPO), constitutional AI, and human-in-the-loop systems, while analyzing their trade-offs in scalability, performance, safety, and implementation complexity.

The paper argues that AI alignment is not solely a technical optimization problem, but a broader socio-technical challenge involving questions of value representation, accountability, fairness, cultural relativism, privacy, and long-term societal impact. It highlights how the growing scarcity of high-quality training data has elevated the importance of human feedback and expert judgment in shaping next-generation AI systems. At the same time, it examines emerging risks such as reward hacking, distribution shift, adversarial manipulation, value lock-in, and scalable oversight limitations, positioning alignment as a critical frontier for the safe deployment of increasingly capable AI systems.

Intended for researchers, policymakers, technologists, and industry practitioners, the paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of AI alignment while identifying future research directions in mechanistic interpretability, adaptive alignment, multi-agent systems, governance frameworks, and aligned AGI development. Rather than presenting a single dominant solution, the paper concludes that effective alignment will likely depend on combining multiple methodologies within carefully designed institutional, technical, and ethical frameworks capable of evolving alongside increasingly advanced AI capabilities.

title: Marketplace Integration and Rating Inflation: Evidence from Online Review Platforms
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong,  and University of Wisconsin-Madison - Wisconsin School of Business

detail.title: Marketplace Integration and Rating Inflation: Evidence from Online Review Platforms
detail.abstract: Online review platforms may monetize their user bases through marketplace integration, allowing brands to sell products directly through the platform. Such marketplace integration may affect reviews through two channels: by creating direct commercial incentives for manipulation and through changes in the composition of contributors. This study examines how marketplace integration through product onboarding affects product reviews. We examine these mechanisms on a leading K-beauty review platform that introduced a transaction marketplace. Leveraging the staggered onboarding of products for sale and granular review and clickstream data, we estimate the effects of product onboarding on subsequent review generation. We find that product onboarding increases review volume and inflates average ratings. Also, new reviews are less informative: they are shorter, contain fewer photos, and are written with less effort. We find no evidence that rating inflation results from seller manipulation, platform-led solicitation through product trials, or reviews by verified purchasers. Instead, onboarding changes who contributes reviews. It attracts more first-time and non-dedicated reviewers while reducing the share of dedicated, experienced reviewers. Because first-time reviewers tend to give higher ratings than dedicated reviewers, this compositional shift produces aggregate rating inflation. Our findings highlight an important consequence of marketplace integration: it can reshape user participation, leading to higher aggregate ratings and less informative reviews even in the absence of manipulation by sellers or the platform.

title: AI and Blockchain: Balancing Risk, Value, and Accountability
affiliations: The Digital Economist

detail.title: AI and Blockchain: Balancing Risk, Value, and Accountability
detail.abstract:
AI and Blockchain: Balancing Risk, Value, and Accountability examines how the convergence of artificial intelligence and blockchain is reshaping enterprise decision-making, automation, trust, and governance. As AI systems become increasingly capable of generating recommendations, executing actions, and operating through autonomous agents, organizations are confronting a new challenge: how to maintain accountability, control, and trust in environments where decisions and transactions increasingly occur at machine speed.

The paper argues that AI and blockchain are not simply parallel technologies, but complementary capabilities. AI can enhance prediction, automate complex workflows, and expand access to specialized capabilities. Blockchain-based trust infrastructure can provide identity, verification, auditability, and tamper-resistant recordkeeping. Together, these technologies can help organizations compress the distance between decision, execution, and accountability while creating new opportunities for efficiency, transparency, and value creation.

At the same time, this convergence changes the governance equation. As AI moves beyond decision support and increasingly participates in autonomous execution, traditional oversight models built around periodic review, human intervention, and retrospective control may prove insufficient. Boards, executives, and institutions remain accountable even when operational decisions occur in seconds. The paper explores the resulting governance challenges, including agent oversight, identity and permissioning, auditability, operational resilience, second-order risk, and the design of trust architectures capable of embedding control directly into machine-speed systems.

Drawing on insights from leaders in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, enterprise technology, and digital infrastructure, the paper provides a governance framework for balancing innovation with accountability. It offers practical guidance for boards, executives, policymakers, and technology leaders seeking to capture the benefits of AI and blockchain while maintaining trust, resilience, transparency, and fiduciary accountability in an increasingly autonomous digital economy.

title: Digital practice differs between allied health professions: a task-level survey of digital work in clinical practice
affiliations: University of Winchester, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Winchester

detail.title: Digital practice differs between allied health professions: a task-level survey of digital work in clinical practice
detail.abstract: BackgroundThe allied health professions (AHPs) are a group of distinct professions with different scopes and documentation duties, yet national electronic health record (EHR) data report them as one aggregated group. Aggregation may conceal meaningful differences in task use, relevance and support needs, which remain unquantified in the UK.ObjectiveTo measure task-level digital practice across AHP professions and identify profession-level differences that remained after correction for multiple comparisons.MethodsA profession-stratified cross-sectional census-frame survey of AHPs at an English specialist cancer centre running a single organisation-wide EHR, using the newly developed AHP Digital Practice Inventory, a provisional 56-task, nine-domain instrument. Analysis was non-parametric with effect sizes and correction for multiple comparisons.Results131 of 363 AHPs (36%) identified a profession or role category and 90 answered at least one task item, with response rates varying substantially by profession. Profession was the only grouping variable producing corrected group differences; band, setting and role type produced none, although one band correlation survived. Transfer-of-care frequency was the largest domain effect (η2_H 0.455) and the only one of 168 tests to clear Bonferroni; documentation personalisation, a feature item, was larger still (0.513). Seven effects survived correction (0.20 to 0.51), all concentrated in task frequency, relevance and feature use. No corrected profession difference was detected in self-rated proficiency or perceived impact. The corrected differences may reflect workflow, scope and local feature provisioning rather than professional capability. A pre-specified rule identified four profession-task combinations frequently performed yet rated below competent that disappeared when professions were pooled.ConclusionsDigital practice appeared more consistently structured by profession than by band, setting or role type, and the differences concentrated on which tasks professions use and value. Organisations should examine workflow, feature provisioning and access before applying generic AHP-wide training and system configuration and optimisation.

title: Inclusive Intelligence: AI-Enabled Career Coaching for Neurodivergent Professionals With ADHD
affiliations: , San Diego State University, San Diego State University, Fowler College of Business, San Diego State University and Fowler College of Business, San Diego State University

detail.title: Inclusive Intelligence: AI-Enabled Career Coaching for Neurodivergent Professionals With ADHD
detail.abstract: This study addresses a core Information Systems design challenge: how to configure AI-enabled support systems for professionals whose cognitive patterns diverge from dominant organizational norms. Using ADHD as a boundary case, it develops and evaluates a design logic for inclusive AI-mediated career coaching. A progressive three-study design moves from problem specification to design articulation to artifact evaluation. Study I identifies ADHD-specific ad hoc support contexts. Study II derives communicative heuristics that make guidance cognitively accessible, actionable, and affectively attuned. Study III instantiates these heuristics in a prompt-conditioned, LLM-based coaching artifact and evaluates it against highly endorsed human responses. This work contributes in two ways. First, it develops design knowledge for configuring inclusive AI support systems by linking support contexts, communicative affordances, and artifact configuration. Second, it shows that AI-generated guidance can approximate perceived helpfulness in task-focused contexts while remaining constrained in emotionally sensitive ones, highlighting cognitive fit, trust calibration, and perceptual alignment.

title: From Mobile Banking to the Digital Banking Ecosystem: Reassessment of a Doctoral Framework

detail.title: From Mobile Banking to the Digital Banking Ecosystem: Reassessment of a Doctoral Framework
detail.abstract: This article offers a critical reassessment and an updated perspective on a doctoral model examining the adoption, user experience, satisfaction, and continuance intention associated with mobile banking services in Morocco. The original findings identified perceived security, usability, and utilitarian value as the primary drivers of adoption, while demonstrating that the cognitive, affective, and hedonic dimensions of the user experience significantly influence customer satisfaction. A critical comparison of these findings with research published since 2020 confirms the robustness of several of these determinants, while also revealing a notable shift in scholarly attention toward trust, adaptation, omnichannel integration, and continuance of use. The analysis further suggests that the principal limitation of the original model now lies in the historical boundaries of its object of study. Mobile banking applications have evolved from being the primary focus of digital banking to becoming one touchpoint within a broader, interconnected ecosystem that is increasingly enhanced by artificial intelligence. Accordingly, the proposed extension shifts the analytical focus from the adoption of a single digital channel to the appropriation of a digital banking ecosystem by incorporating open banking, mobile payment systems, omnichannel customer experience, personalization, and algorithmic trust. The article concludes by outlining a future research agenda and providing a conceptual foundation for subsequent bibliometric analyses of the evolution of digital banking research.

title: Can We Trust Cyber Defence Agents? TrustOps for Evidence Grounded Security Operations
affiliations: Hellenic Open University, Focal Point sprl, University of Piraeus and University of Piraeus

detail.title: Can We Trust Cyber Defence Agents? TrustOps for Evidence Grounded Security Operations
detail.abstract: Agentic AI is moving into security operations. It can triage incidents, plan responses and support cyber defence decisions. But these settings are unforgiving. A wrong action can disrupt a service, enable privilege abuse or leave a threat only partly contained. So the real question is not whether an agent can suggest a response. It is whether an analyst should trust that response. We propose TrustOps, an evidencegrounded trust management framework for agentic cyber defence. TrustOps attaches a trust score to every recommendation, and it computes that score from verifiable evidence: alerts, vulnerabilities, defensive posture, response playbooks and controlled adversary emulation. Four prototype components supply this evidence. Attack surface assessment maps host inventories to CPE, CVE, CWE and CVSS. Posture assessment links assets to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, D3FEND artifacts, detections and mitigations. Security breach simulation reproduces attacker behaviour through controlled emulation. Defensive cyber operations groups MITREtagged alerts and links them to playbooks. A scoring model combines these dimensions, and it lowers the score when evidence is missing, conflicting, stale or of low confidence. We also outline an ATT&CKbased evaluation against LLM-only, playbook-only and vulnerabilityprioritization baselines. The aim is a human-in-the-loop, explainable and evidence-driven cyber defence agent.

title:
When Compliance Becomes a Signal: 
Optical Compliance, Supervisory Design, and the Economics of Evidence

detail.title:
When Compliance Becomes a Signal: 
Optical Compliance, Supervisory Design, and the Economics of Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper argues that firms do not merely respond to regulatory rules; they respond to what supervisors are observed to reward. Where supervisory attention — by regulators over firms, and by second- and third-line functions over the first line — weighs governance artefacts and personal credibility more heavily than independent evidence of operating effectiveness, firms rationally optimise toward the signals being measured, producing what this paper terms optical compliance: the visible appearance of control without its substance. The same mechanism recurs at each layer of the supervisory chain, from the business through compliance and the board to the regulator itself, because every layer's own effectiveness is, in turn, judged partly through governance signals rather than direct observation. This is a variant of Goodhart's Law applied to supervision itself. The paper develops this mechanism across four connected deficiencies — artefact substitution, the credibility trap, episodic "tsunami-like" supervision, and the feedback loop that turns supervisory habit into industry best practice — before arguing that AI-enabled monitoring is beginning to change the underlying economics by sharply reducing the cost of operating evidence, and therefore the value of credibility as a substitute for it. The paper closes with implications for C-suite strategy and a stakeholder-by-stakeholder response, from the regulator through to the embedded risk advisor.

title:
Execution Efficiency as a Cost-reduction Mechanism in U.S. Supply Chain Industries: 
An Operational Governance Framework

detail.title:
Execution Efficiency as a Cost-reduction Mechanism in U.S. Supply Chain Industries: 
An Operational Governance Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study did not involve human participants, personal data, or identifiable organizational data. The analysis is based on conceptual modeling and synthetic simulation scenarios.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Supply chain inefficiencies in the United States continue to generate excessive delays, rework, and operational costs despite widespread adoption of digital visibility and monitoring systems. These inefficiencies stem not from a lack of data, but from weak execution governance and delayed follow-up mechanisms across multi-tier supply chain networks. This study proposes an operational governance framework that positions execution efficiency as a primary mechanism for time and cost reduction in U.S. supply chain industries. Adopting a conceptual and architecture-driven research design, the study develops the Architectural Logic of Zero-Trust Networks (ZTN-AL) as a continuous verification and follow-up governance mechanism for multi-tier supply chains. The framework is operationalized through a Zero-Trust Supply Chain Architecture and an orchestration model that enables real-time identity verification, segmented access control, and adaptive policy enforcement across distributed supply chain nodes. A simulated multi-echelon risk scenario is used to compare the proposed framework with a baseline visibility-based governance model using Breach Containment Time (BCT) and Data Integrity Stability (DIS) as execution performance indicators. The simulation results indicate that execution efficiency achieved through continuous verification can substantially reduce response delays, follow-up lag, and coordination failures, resulting in substantial time savings and indirect cost reduction across supply chain operations. By reframing execution governance as a cost-reduction mechanism rather than a compliance function, this study contributes a transferable operational framework applicable to U.S. supply chain industries seeking to improve performance under high-cost and high-complexity conditions.

title: Hotelling's Lemma under Imperfect Competition: The Firm-Level Supply Function as a Pricing-Strategy Parameter
affiliations: University of Turku - Turku School of Economics

detail.title: Hotelling's Lemma under Imperfect Competition: The Firm-Level Supply Function as a Pricing-Strategy Parameter
detail.abstract: In the standard theory of the firm, a supply function (a schedule showing how much a firm will sell at each price) is defined only for the price-taking firm of perfect competition. Under monopoly and oligopoly the textbooks say that no supply curve exists, and the firm's optimum is described as a single point. This note argues that the claim is too strong. If the firm holds a belief about how steeply its sales fall when it raises price, then profit maximisation gives it a welldefined rule connecting quantity to price, and that rule is a supply function. The rule turns out to be a direct generalisation of Hotelling's lemma, the classical result that the competitive firm's supply is the derivative of its profit function with respect to price. Three consequences follow. First, the responsiveness of this supply schedule to price has a closed form, and can be negative: a firm facing constant-elasticity demand with constant marginal cost has a supply schedule that slopes downward. Second, multiplying the schedule by a single scalar produces a family of supply strategies that reproduces the familiar Cournot and Stackelberg duopoly solutions, gives a determinate answer to the case in which both duopolists try to lead, and corresponds one-to-one to the "conduct parameter" that empirical industrial economists estimate from data. Third, because a pricing algorithm is itself a rule that maps market conditions into a price, the same scalar measures how aggressively an algorithm competes, and it can be inferred from prices and costs without access to the algorithm's code. This offers competition authorities an outcomebased complement to the code-level audits proposed in the recent literature on algorithmic collusion. The results were first derived in a 1994 monograph and are restated here in the light of current work on markups, conduct and algorithmic pricing.

title: From Copyright to "Copyhope": On Protecting Software IP in the Age of A.I
affiliations: Principal Data Scientist, Fulcrumbright

detail.title: From Copyright to "Copyhope": On Protecting Software IP in the Age of A.I
detail.abstract:
In September 2023, we published Test Driving Code Llama-2 [TEST-LLAMA-2], examining
the capabilities and limitations of A.I.-based code generation. At that time, we
observed that while Large Language Models could produce reasonable-looking
code, they demonstrated fundamental gaps in understanding efficiency, correctness,
and architectural considerations. We concluded the future was exciting but cautioned
that A.I. tools would likely produce average-quality code converging on statistical
consensus rather than excellence.

Three years hence, these hurdles have largely been overcome. A.I. models now
generate near production-ready code albeit with expert guidance, yet the legal
hurdles have grown more formidable. The central question emerges: How does one
protect software intellectual property when copyright law no longer applies to A.I.-
generated outputs?

This paper explores the evolution from traditional copyright protection to what we
term “Copyhope”— attaching licenses not because they are enforceable today, but in
anticipation that the law will eventually catch up. We examine why copyright fails for
A.I. outputs, the limitations of contract law in seamless downloads, and present a
Contract-First & Confidentiality Code Preamble along with the Operational
Elements and Intellectual Property Strategy required to make it legally viable. We
posit that the all-familiar copyright preamble found in thousands of Github
repositories which simply said “Copyright © <year> <name> - All Rights Reserved”
has come of age and is in need not of revision, but of revolution.
From the onset, I would like to state that I am not a lawyer –-- only fond of the law. I
am not qualified to give legal advice. As such, the content of this paper is only my
personal opinion --- please refer to the section “Legal Disclaimer” for the full
disclaimer which applies to this paper in its entirety.

The future is not merely exciting—it is legally transformative.

title: A Quantitative Context-aware Data Reliability Scoring Model for Trustworthy AI Decision-making in Critical Infrastructure

detail.title: A Quantitative Context-aware Data Reliability Scoring Model for Trustworthy AI Decision-making in Critical Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The increasing reliance on artificial intelligence (AI) for making decisions in critical infrastructure is based on data obtained from sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, operational technology, communication networks, and external information sources. Yet, data that is inaccurate, incomplete, inconsistent, outdated, or not appropriate in a given context can compromise the reliability of AI systems which are otherwise quite sophisticated. Current data trust and quality models usually focus on individual aspects of reliability without offering an integrated and context-sensitive evaluation of data reliability (Matei and Patriciu, 2025; Nastoska et al., 2025; Rafiq, Jarir and Asri, 2025). This study presents a quantitative Context-Aware Data Reliability Scoring Model to help with trustworthy AI decision-making in critical infrastructure. A systematic review of the relevant literature is carried out to identify the key dimensions of data reliability and to combine them into a normalized, weighted scoring system that takes into account context, uncertainty, and multidimensional reliability, rather than viewing data quality as fixed. The literature synthesis enables the development of an integrated reliability model that includes accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, provenance, integrity, uncertainty, and contextual relevance. The proposed framework also recommends that data reliability should be continuously evaluated in relation to the operational context and uncertainty during the entire AI decision-making process. As a result, reliability should not be considered a one-time property carried out during preprocessing but should be treated as a dynamic input that affects the interpretation, prediction, and trustworthiness of AI-supported decisions in critical infrastructure (Chatziamanetoglou and Rantos, 2025; Pérez-Rosero et al., 2026; Cardenas et al., 2025).

title: Stochastic MILP Optimization for Co-Located PV-BESS Assets: Managing Imbalance Tail Risks via CVaR and Piecewise Degradation in the German Power Market

detail.title: Stochastic MILP Optimization for Co-Located PV-BESS Assets: Managing Imbalance Tail Risks via CVaR and Piecewise Degradation in the German Power Market
detail.abstract: Co-located Photovoltaic (PV) and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) face substantial financial exposure in modern deregulated power markets due to high day-ahead forecast uncertainty and volatile real-time imbalance settlement mechanisms (e.g., the German reBAP system). In this paper, we propose a two-stage Stochastic Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation that optimizes day-ahead nomination commitments while explicitly mitigating physical and financial risks. The model incorporates: (i) a piecewise linear approximation of depth-ofdischarge (DoD) degradation costs constrained by manufacturer Equivalent Full Cycle (EFC) warranty ceilings, and (ii) a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaRα) risk metric (α = 0.95) to hedge against severe adverse imbalance penalty realizations. Backtesting using empirical generation profiles from the German Bundesnetzagentur (SMARD) platform demonstrates that the proposed framework prevents aggressive cyclic overutilization and delivers optimal risk-adjusted profitability.

title: Work-Life Boundaries in Hybrid Telework: Role Strain, Digital Intrusion, and Boundary Management -exploratory Evidence from Greece

detail.title: Work-Life Boundaries in Hybrid Telework: Role Strain, Digital Intrusion, and Boundary Management -exploratory Evidence from Greece

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No institutional ethics-committee or review-board approval was obtained for this study. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, and participants were informed that the data would be used for academic purposes and consented on that basis. No identifiable participant information or verbatim qualitative responses are included in the manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Telework has become a routine arrangement rather than an exceptional one, and the boundary between paid work and the rest of life is now negotiated daily rather than fixed by the working day. This exploratory study examines how employees in predominantly lowintensity hybrid arrangements in Greece describe that negotiation. Eighteen employees completed a self-administered online questionnaire comprising 49 numbered itemsnine closed demographic questions, two short free-text demographic questions, one closed item on preferred working arrangement and 37 open-ended narrative questionsfollowed by a twelve-item Likert battery developed for this study. Free-text responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and are reported here as anonymized thematic paraphrase; Likert responses were analyzed with non-parametric statistics, and five theoretically motivated associations were selected for focused exploratory analysis with permutationbased robustness checks. Participants described boundaries as fluid rather than as a chosen position, and, where they described expectations as unclear, located the unclarity in the end of the working day and in availability rather than in task expectations, which most described as clear. Role strain was positively associated with digital intrusion (ρ = .69), and negatively associated with perceived respect for the boundaries the employee had set (ρ =-.68) and with psychological detachment (ρ =-.64); all three were stable under permutation inference and case deletion. Reported use of boundary-closing strategies showed no association with role strain (ρ =-.13, p = .60), but no participant disagreed with that Likert item even though three described in free text that they had no such practices or could not apply them, so the null is weakly identified and should not be read as evidence that such strategies are ineffective. Technical or training support was the most commonly described form of organizational provision, though it was not universal, and no participant identified a dedicated psychological or wellbeing provision. The whole analysis is exploratory. The sample is small, purposively sampled and male-skewed, the measures are researcherdeveloped and unvalidated, analysis was carried out by a single researcher, and the design is cross-sectional. Findings should be read as descriptive of this sample and as a basis for better-instrumented work.

title: Pareto Efficiency in the Two-stage Adaptive Robust Resource-constrained Project Scheduling Problem
affiliations: and University of Calabria

detail.title: Pareto Efficiency in the Two-stage Adaptive Robust Resource-constrained Project Scheduling Problem
detail.abstract: We introduce the concept of Pareto efficiency into the two-stage adaptive robust resource-constrained project scheduling problem. In this setting, multiple optimal first-stage decisions often exist, all sharing the same worst-case makespan but potentially exhibiting substantially different performance under non-worst-case scenarios. We address this issue by formalizing Pareto efficiency within this problem setting and defining four Pareto relations among optimal solutions. To determine these relations, we propose two feasibility programs, develop an algorithm to verify whether a given optimal solution is Pareto-efficient, and present an algorithm to generate an inclusion-minimal Pareto-efficient optimal solution. To increase the probability of generating Pareto-efficient optimal solutions, we introduce two penalty-based models, TCC and DUR, which encourage sparser transitive closures or discourage connections between activities with longer durations. Computational experiments demonstrate that TCC and DUR produce significantly more Pareto-efficient optimal solutions than the default output of the SCIP solver, as further confirmed by a logistic regression with generalized estimating equations.

title: Mental Accounting and Remittance Dependency Among Afghan Households: A Behavioural Finance Perspective
affiliations: University of Mysore, India, Maulana Azad National Urdu University and Babasaheb Bhim Rao Ambedkar University

detail.title: Mental Accounting and Remittance Dependency Among Afghan Households: A Behavioural Finance Perspective
detail.abstract: This study investigated the influence of the dimensions of mental accounting on remittance dependency among Afghan households. Mental accounting was conceptualized as a multidimensional construct comprising mental accounting labelling (MAL), mental budgeting (MB), and Fungibility bias (FB). Using a quantitative research design, data were collected from 317 households through a structured 4-points Likertscale questionnaire. The data were analyzed using structural equation modelling (SEM) to examine the relationship between dimensions of mental accounting and remittance dependency (RD). The findings indicated that only mental accounting labelling exhibited a significant positive relationship with remittance dependency (β = 0.537, p < 0.001), whereas Fungibility Bias (β = 0.096, p < 0.05) and Mental Budgeting (β =-0.029, p = 0.708) did not illustrate statistically significant association. These findings indicate that the dimensions of mental accounting do not contribute equally to explaining remittance dependency behavior among the sampled Afghan households. The study also found that remittances are primarily allocated to the consumption category of the households, particularly for daily needs, healthcare and urgent financial needs, while only a limited proportion was allocated toward productive categories such as investment and trade. Overall, the findings suggest that household's mentally categorize and manage remittance income differently from their ordinary sources of income, consistent with core theory of mental accounting. The study emphasizes the importance of understanding behavioral biases, particularly mental accounting and its dimensions, as well as remittance use when designing financial literacy initiatives and remittance management policies for similar households' populations.

title: Energy Markets Under Chokepoint Stress: the 2026 Hormuz Shock
affiliations: , Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Banca d’Italia and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Energy Markets Under Chokepoint Stress: the 2026 Hormuz Shock
detail.abstract: We analyze the energy-market consequences of the 2026 Middle East conflict and the associated disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict created the largest physical supply disruption in the history of global energy markets, with effects extending beyond crude oil to refined products, petrochemical feedstocks and liquefied natural gas. Energy prices rose sharply, but less than the scale of the physical disruption alone would have suggested, thanks to prewar high inventories, emergency stock releases, the rerouting of commodity flows, and demand compression. The shock was global but differed from previous energy shocks along several dimensions: its unprecedented size, its propagation across refined product markets, the asymmetric exposure of Asian and European importers, and its uncertain persistence especially regarding the restoration of Hormuz flows and damaged infrastructure. Compared with the 2021-22 European energy crisis, the 2026 episode affected oil and gas more homogeneously and it was more global than regional.

title: Mediated Relationships between External Environment and Internal Environment and Adopting Islamic Financial Transactions
affiliations: University of Benghazi and International Islamic University of Malaysia (IIUM) - IIUM Institute of Islamic Banking and Finance

detail.title: Mediated Relationships between External Environment and Internal Environment and Adopting Islamic Financial Transactions
detail.abstract: Purpose-This paper sought to investigate the mediated links between the external environment and the adaptation of the internal environment in the context of commercial banks adopting Islamic financial activities.By providing a conceptual framework that includes all external environmental factors affecting commercial banks, rather than focusing solely on the preferences of bank users. Design/methodology/approach-In line with the conceptual framework, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) has been employed to depict and test the hypothesized relationships among observed variables quantitatively. A questionnaire was designed and distributed to 14 commercial banks in Libya. The sample unit was represented by managers, directors of departments, and personnel. Statistically, the two-step approach of the SEM was used. The first step is evaluating SEM measures by carrying out the measurement model CFA (first-order) and CFA (second-order) on the conceptual construct of measurements. The second step is testing the study hypotheses by carrying out the overall structural equation modeling. Findings-The results illustrated the mediated relationships between the internal and external environments regarding the adoption of Islamic financial transactions by commercial banks. Notably, the CFA estimates indicated that the adoption by Libyan commercial banks was more strongly associated with the external environment as a factor of institutional constraints rather than as a catalyst for change. Originality/value-In the context of institutional thought, this study designed a theoretical framework that involves all main actors surrounding an organization's organizational field. Therefore, this article is a step forward in filling up a scientific gap declared by Alvesson and Spicer (2019) and Suddaby et al. (2010), namely, binding organizations with their broader organizational field and societal environment. According to Suddaby et al., "the challenge ahead is for researchers to examine organizations as mediators and lenses of their institutional environments and the reciprocal co-construction of organizations and their institutional environments." Hence, the implications of the current search may open up new horizons to advance the scientific research to provide an integrated approach to examining the relationship between the organization's internal and external environments to bond the organization's capacity with its organizational field systematically.

title: ES Activities and Labor Productivity: Evidence from Korean Manufacturing Firms
affiliations: Bank of Korea and The Bank of Korea

detail.title: ES Activities and Labor Productivity: Evidence from Korean Manufacturing Firms

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Korea Economic Research Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study empirically examines how firms’ environmental and social (E and S) activities affect labor productivity using E and S metrics provided by the Korea Corporate Governance Service (KCGS). Using a panel of listed firms over 2015–2023, we find that both the ES rating and the ES score are significantly and negatively associated with labor productivity, which remains robust when we use the overall ESG rating or the E and S pillar ratings. We further provide channel evidence consistent with a cost-burden mechanism: firms with higher ES exhibit a higher total operating cost ratio (TOCR), suggesting that the ES–productivity relationship may be linked to operating cost pressure. Subcategory analyses reveal heterogeneous pathways within ES. In the environmental category, operational/management and communication-oriented activities are negatively related to labor productivity, consistent with higher coordination and management costs. In contrast, community engagement in the social category is positively related to labor productivity, pointing to a complementary pathway through trust, reputation, and relationship capital. Finally, firm- and industry-level analyses indicate substantial heterogeneity in the ES–productivity relationship across firms and industries. Overall, by combining cost-based channel evidence, subcategory-level decompositions, and heterogeneity analyses, this study highlights that evaluating the economic implications of sustainability initiatives requires attention not only to aggregate ES/ESG metrics but also to cost structure, activity types, and firm and industry characteristics.

title: Geopolitics and Export Miracles: Firm-level Evidence from U.S. War Procurement in Korea
affiliations: , ,  and University of Oxford, Saïd Business School

detail.title: Geopolitics and Export Miracles: Firm-level Evidence from U.S. War Procurement in Korea
detail.abstract: How did geopolitics shape East Asia’s economic development? We find that U.S. military procurement during the Vietnam War---a shock which peaked at nearly 3% of South Korean GDP, rivaling the Marshall Plan---catalyzed Korea’s export-led industrialization. We construct a new firm-level dataset that matches Korean export records with U.S. procurement contracts awarded between 1965 and 1973 to estimate the causal impact of winning a contract on export performance. A firm winning its first contract raises its likelihood of exporting by 14.7 percentage points and its export value by 40%. Treated firms are more likely to expand into third-country markets and export manufacturing products---and these gains are unlikely to come from business stealing. Finally, we find that U.S. procurement and domestic industrial policy were likely complementary. Our findings reveal a neglected channel through which Cold War geopolitics shaped the East Asian economic miracle.

title: Assembly Accuracy Prediction Model for Rigid-flexible Coupled Multi-body Systems under Optional Processes
affiliations: Jilin University, Jilin University, Jilin University, Jilin University and Jilin University

detail.title: Assembly Accuracy Prediction Model for Rigid-flexible Coupled Multi-body Systems under Optional Processes
detail.abstract: High-precision industrial product manufacturing imposes rigorous accuracy requirements. Merely upgrading component machining accuracy results in an exponential surge in manufacturing costs. To address this practical dilemma, academic research has gradually shifted focus from pure machining optimization to Assembly process exploration. Nevertheless, existing assembly process studies predominantly concentrate on tolerance design, with insufficient investigations into the effects of assembly methods on assembly accuracy. Against this backdrop, this paper proposes a Monte Carlo simulation-based method for assembly accuracy prediction under selective assembly. Furthermore, most conventional parallel error propagation models for assembly systems rely on rigid-body assumptions, which fail to account for error decrease and amplification induced by component deformation during parallel error propagation. To remedy this research deficiency, this paper develops a novel flexible screw theory model for parallel error propagation based on the minimum potential energy principle. Taking the dual-axis rotary table of a five-axis machine tool as the research object, the validity and feasibility of the proposed model are verified via simulation analysis. This study fills the research gap concerning the influence of assembly methods on assembly accuracy, and provides a solid theoretical foundation for the collaborative optimization of tolerance design and assembly method formulation in precision manufacturing.

title: Neurological Perspectives on Organisational Flexibility:How Brain Science Can Inform Crisis Management
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Neurological Perspectives on Organisational Flexibility:How Brain Science Can Inform Crisis Management
detail.abstract: Organisational science's longstanding dilemma becomes apparent during periods of crisis. Organisations should respond ideally during times of uncertainty but the people behind these organisations have biological limitations which make them less adaptable, threat sensitive and narrow-minded exactly when adaptability is necessary. Although organisational resilience has received much attention in terms of structure and behaviour, there hasn't been much focus on the neural basis of adaptability in the form of collective action. This essay aims at presenting a neuroscientific account of organisational adaptability and crisis management as an emergent process of interrelated neural systems for prediction, attention, emotional regulation and social coordination.Based on predictive processing theories and the dynamics of brain networks, we model organisational flexibility as a distributed cognitive system whose adaptability follows the same principles of neural integration and plasticity. We examine the interplay of brain networks involved in executive control, salience processing, and emotional threat processing to explain decision-making under uncertainty and time pressure and argue that flexible interplay among these brain networks, rather than executive control, determines the brain's ability to reweight prediction error, regulate stress and switch between exploration and exploitation modes.Through the synthesis of insights from cognitive neuroscience, computational psychiatry and social neuroscience, this review connects the micro-mechanisms of neural computations and the macro-mechanisms of organizational behavior, thus producing empirically testable propositions regarding the relationship between neuro-flexibility and leadership effectiveness, teamwork and organizational resilience, and translating these into frameworks that utilize behavioral experimentation, psychophysiological measurements and computational modeling of adaptive decision-making systems.

title: The Structural Ceiling: Informality, Broken Monetary Transmission, and the Persistence of Sovereign Currency Mismatches
affiliations: Blantyre International University

detail.title: The Structural Ceiling: Informality, Broken Monetary Transmission, and the Persistence of Sovereign Currency Mismatches

detail.abstract: Mainly macroeconomic suggests that “Original Sin,” the inability of sovereign nations to borrow foreign capital in their domestic currencies, can be successfully targeted through structural reforms namely, inflation targeting, institutional strengthening, and the deepening of domestic bond markets. This paper does not dispute that framework on its own terms. Instead, it specifies a boundary condition the framework has not yet been tested against the structural ceiling of informality. I point out that the three-pillar model is well matched to economies with a sufficiently formalized financial system, but that in economies where informal activity dominates daily economic life, the monetary transmission mechanism the model depends on is structurally absent, so the same three levers largely fail to operate. To establish this boundary condition, I built around a reverse stress test and scenario-based analysis tracing how a sovereign debt shock travels from the balance sheet down to the street level under two contrasting structural configurations a highly formalized economy, illustrated by Greece, and highly informal frontier economies, anchored analytically by Zimbabwe alongside structural insights from Malawi, Zambia, and Ghana. Greece did not meet Original Sin's strict technical definition, since its debt and its revenue were both denominated in the Euro, but it exhibited the same clinical presentation and required almost the same prescription, having surrendered the capacity to devalue or act as its own lender of last resort. Notably, Greece was hit harder and faster than its informal counterparts precisely because its formalized economy lacked the informal cushion this paper identifies as central to frontier-economy resilience. When an informality threshold of roughly sixty percent and above, economic activity, inflationtargeting rate hikes stop stabilising the currency and instead escalate the sovereign's own domestic debt-servicing costs; that this produces a procyclical trap in which anti-inflation policy degrades the very fiscal base it is meant to protect; and that the informal “trust-buffer” networks cushioning households during a formal-sector freeze are themselves subject to an abrupt collapse beyond which they fail systemically rather than gradually. Taken together, these findings suggest that Han, Lee, and Oh's (2024) dissipation pathway is a credible account of how sufficiently formalized emerging markets escape Original Sin, but is not yet a general theory: for the majority of the developing world, the structural ceiling of informality must be addressed before the three pillars can function as intended.

title: From Contract to Legal Consequences: Mapping the Structure of Legal Research on Smart Contracts Using OpenAlex and VOSviewer

detail.title: From Contract to Legal Consequences: Mapping the Structure of Legal Research on Smart Contracts Using OpenAlex and VOSviewer
detail.abstract: Legal scholarship on smart contracts is commonly organised around the question of contractual status. Keyword co-occurrence mapping is used here to test whether noncontractual reasoning has developed into a distinct research stream or remains distributed across several legal domains. OpenAlex records retrieved on 24 August 2026 were analysed in VOSviewer. The broader search identified 40,290 works on smart contracts, of which 10,400 matched a legal query; a more focused corpus of 1,000 works addressed legal nature, validity, and contractual status. Applying a minimum occurrence threshold of six and a thesaurus-based cleaning process produced a network of 170 keywords in seven clusters. Contract doctrine forms a recognisable cluster around privity of contract, breach of contract, obligation, frustration of purpose, and severability. By contrast, property rights, consumer protection, liability, tort, intermediary, automation, and dispute resolution are dispersed across several clusters. The overlay map also places a number of liability, userprotection, and remedial topics in more recent publication periods than several traditional contract-law themes. The pattern does not support the existence of an autonomous noncontractual school. It instead indicates a broader reorientation of smart-contract scholarship toward the legal consequences of automated execution: the allocation of rights, responsibility, risk, and remedies beyond the question of contractual classification.

title: The Depreciation Paradox: Accelerator Obsolescence, the Structural Collateral Floor, and the Safe Limits of AI Infrastructure Leverage
affiliations: and New Jersey Institute of Technology

detail.title: The Depreciation Paradox: Accelerator Obsolescence, the Structural Collateral Floor, and the Safe Limits of AI Infrastructure Leverage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors are affiliated with Origin AI. The views expressed in this paper are the authors' own and are not those of Origin AI. The authors hold no financial interest in any company or facility named in this paper, and received no compensation from any party with an interest in its findings.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study analyses publicly available regulatory filings, official statistical publications, published benchmark results and vendor documentation. It involves no human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted by the authors without external funding.

detail.abstract: Data centre operators are financing artificial-intelligence accelerators with secured debt while lengthening the accounting lives they assign to them. This paper measures the gap and shows what it implies for collateral. Two independent measurements of the obsolescence hazard agree in order of magnitude and disagree in level: the Bureau of Economic Analysis age-price profile for computing equipment implies a geometric rate of 0.5002 yr−1 , while the audited MLPerf Training lineage from V100 to GB300 implies 0.3339 yr−1 from 6 generational steps over 6.38 years. Against either benchmark the depreciation wedge Δ = 𝜙 − 1/𝜏acct is positive for all 10 filers in a hand-adjudicated panel of 67 primary filer-years, and among the 6 filers with an unbroken record the median disclosed life has moved from 3.00 to 6.00 years since 2018, with no measured slowing of the hazard behind it. One filer attributes a shortening of a named subset of servers to “the increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning” while leaving the class life unchanged, so the direction of travel in disclosed lives understates the direction of travel in disclosed reasoning. The paper then asks what a hazard of this size does to secured borrowing. A lender who must stay covered at every future date faces a collateral floor 𝜃max (𝑎) = 𝜅𝑒−𝑔(𝑎) whose derivative at origination is unbounded, so the constraint is slack exactly where it is tested and binds at a strictly interior age. The floor is worst at 𝑎 ∗ , returns to 𝜅 at exactly 4𝑎 ∗ , and beyond that age does not bind at all; written in 𝑤 = √ 𝑎/𝑎 ∗ its shape is exp[−𝑔(𝑎 ∗ ) 𝑤(2 − 𝑤)] for every admissible calibration, so one scalar fixes the entire profile. The safe origination advance is therefore 𝜅𝑒−𝑔(𝑎 ∗ ) rather than 𝜅. At a calibration whose arrival process is measured and whose loan terms are stated (a 3-year facility amortising to a fifteen percent balloon), a 60 percent recovery rate supports an advance of only 35.1 percent of value, with the worst case falling at 1.80 years, inside the facility’s own life. Inverting the constraint on disclosed facility terms recovers the obsolescence rate those terms implicitly assume, which is the paper’s main diagnostic: it can be computed for any borrower from public documents and compared with 𝜙.

title: The Same-Model Ceiling: Testing Multi-Model AI Review in Strategic Analysis

detail.title: The Same-Model Ceiling: Testing Multi-Model AI Review in Strategic Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Richard Foster-Fletcher is the founder of MKAI and Reality & Reason. This research was conducted independently and received no third-party funding.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study used a constructed case and language models; it involved no human participants, personal data or patient information. The language models described in the paper served as research instruments and also supported study administration, verification, workbook preparation and drafting. Richard Foster-Fletcher designed the study, reviewed the research materials and accepts responsibility for the analysis and paper.

detail.abstract: This study tests whether adding different AI models to the review of a strategic analysis finds important issues that repeated reviews by the original model still miss. Claude Opus 5 produced twelve analyses of one constructed acquisition case. Each analysis then received six critiques under the same brief: three from fresh Claude sessions and three from GPT-5.6 Sol, Muse Spark 1.2 and DeepSeek V4 Pro. Across the twelve tasks, the reviewers raised 216 possible omissions. After claims depending on unverified outside information were excluded, 152 remained. These were compared blind and combined when they described the same issue. The same-model and multi-model reviews shared 25 issues. The same-model reviews found 18 further issues, while the multi-model panel found 37. Every task contained at least one issue found only by the multi-model panel. Claude then assessed whether the 37 additional issues mattered. It judged that 35 would change proposed terms, evidence requirements or commitment conditions. No single issue changed the toplevel decision route, although combining several issues changed that route in three tasks. Two further models compared each revision with the original in a blind assessment, with a third model resolving disagreement. The revision was preferred in eight of twelve tasks, the original in one, and three comparisons ended in ties. For this case and model panel, changing the reviewers widened the analysis even though the number of critiques and the review brief stayed constant.

title: How Can Autonomous Vehicles Avoid Crashes? Comparative Insights from Generative AI Responses based on Collision Type and Mode of Operation
affiliations: , South Carolina State University, University of North Florida, Florida International University (FIU), Tennessee State University and Texas A&M Transportation Institute

detail.title: How Can Autonomous Vehicles Avoid Crashes? Comparative Insights from Generative AI Responses based on Collision Type and Mode of Operation
detail.abstract: Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) are revolutionizing transportation operations and safety as the absence of drivers in AVs is expected to eliminate most driver-related errors. However, crashes involving AVs continue to increase in various parts of the world partly due to operating in mixed traffic. The most recent statistics show that there were about 700 crashes involving AVs in California between 2014 and 2024. Various researchers have been investigating the nature and other characteristics of AV-related crashes to reduce their occurrence using several methodologies, such as data analysis, machine learning, and simulation modeling. In recent years, the evolution of generative AI has supported safety studies by helping researchers analyze crash reports and improve predictive models. This study used ChatGPT and Gemini to examine AV crash narratives from California and propose preventive strategies. Using text network analysis, key themes and relationships within crash narratives were identified, while scatter text plot analysis categorized responses by collision types and modes of operation. ChatGPT emphasized proactive measures, such as activating hazard lights, employing auditory alerts, and enhancing situational awareness, while Gemini prioritized Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), maintaining safe following distances, and leveraging sensor-based technologies. Overall, to avoid a collision, the generative AI tools suggest maintaining proper distance, better use of sensors, and avoiding disengagements. The findings provide operators with an additional layer of insight on how to avoid AV crashes, but they should be used cautiously as some responses may mislead the operators.

title: What a Binary Column cannot Capture Regulatory Architecture and the Attribution of Responsibility in U.S. Auctioneer Licensing

detail.title: What a Binary Column cannot Capture Regulatory Architecture and the Attribution of Responsibility in U.S. Auctioneer Licensing
