detail.abstract:
Ordinary time-to-event controls cannot fully represent the risk of an event-linked perpetual future whose adjudication path may be proposed, disputed, reset, Oracle-final, adapter-terminal, or protocol-final. This paper develops state-triggered margin and settlement controls and formalizes conversion of a synthetic obligation into funded Conditional Tokens Framework claims.

A state-conditioned margin rule combines an adverse-outcome support floor with expected shortfall, execution, finality, and model-risk components. We prove that a common time-only requirement either under-covers the higher-risk state or over-margins the lower-risk state, and that basis funding retains its economic meaning only while an executable mark-index arbitrage loop remains available. The settlement family includes full wait, closing auction, reserve-backed provisional settlement, and claim conversion.

The completed Polymarket finality study supplies an observed calibration layer rather than a hypothetical timing model. Its exact-linked population contains 108,638 conditions. Among 99,283 conditions with an observed protocol resolution, first observed redemption has a Kaplan–Meier median of 182 seconds and first positive-payout redemption a median of 200 seconds under condition-specific right censoring at the 2026-07-12 snapshot. The same data retain long censoring and redemption tails and a large class for which an exact terminal request-generation path is not identified. These findings justify state-qualified controls while sharply limiting any trigger that requires unobserved cross-layer order.

For conversion, a common re-mark and complementary account debits preserve terminal wealth for both long and short positions. The conversion mark cancels, but execution costs and missing collateral remain on an explicit balance sheet. Under the collateral convention inherited from Paper 1, full self-funded conversion above one-times leverage is impossible without top-up, prior deleveraging, reserve capital, credit, or another external funding source. Positionwise feasibility also fails to imply aggregate feasibility when several accounts share one order book or claim inventory.

The empirical closure is a gate result rather than a new seven-configuration performance comparison. An exact condition-ID audit links 837 of the 108,638 Paper 5 conditions to the frozen processed Paper 1 reference layer; within that bridge, 815 have an observed preparation endpoint, 240 an observed condition-resolution endpoint, and 246 a first observed redemption endpoint. The accepted Paper 1 maintenance-path pass, drawdown, P&L, liquidation incidence, and terminal account shortfall tables remain historical mechanical-reference outputs and are not re-estimated here. The available evidence does not contain the path-level PMXT tick/book archive or a recoverable pre-outcome numerical trigger/funding/allocation registry needed to execute the registered configurations C0–C6. Their comparative hypotheses therefore remain not evaluated. This is an evidence-gate disposition, not negative evidence about state-triggered control or conversion.

title: The (Poly)market Price of Weather Risk
affiliations: University of Bologna

detail.title: The (Poly)market Price of Weather Risk
detail.abstract: Weather derivatives are increasingly growing in importance, as the hedging of climate risk factors becomes a priority not only for regulators, but also for players in the energy sector. Their current market is lacking in liquidity, which complicates the valuation of such instruments, as the non-unique pricing measure used by the market cannot be identified precisely. This paper proposes a method to estimate the market price of weather risk from the event probabilities implied by contracts sold on prediction markets. The methodology is applied to temperature markets, finding that the market price of temperature risk is time-varying and also dependent on the strike: it is positive for high-temperature contracts and negative for low-temperature ones, reflecting asymmetric pricing of warming and cooling risk. This pattern holds across seasons, with the highest premium for high minimum temperature contracts. The results reveal a climate risk smirk that parallels the volatility smile in equity options, and document geographical and temporal variability in the pricing of temperature risk.

title: The Formation, Maintenance, and Mobility of Status Hierarchy in High School Football Teams: A Sociological Study of Starter and Substitute Positions

detail.title: The Formation, Maintenance, and Mobility of Status Hierarchy in High School Football Teams: A Sociological Study of Starter and Substitute Positions
detail.abstract: American football is a highly popular sport worldwide. A football team consists of starters and substitutes, with the former accounting for the majority of playing time and enjoying greater prestige and influence within the team. Traditional literature suggests that ability-related factors are the most critical determinants of starter/substitute status, but it underestimates the important role of social factors. Based on Social Stratification Theory, and employing questionnaire surveys and one-on-one interviews, this study collected the perspectives of 25 high school and college varsity football players and two team coaches regarding the determinants of starter/substitute positions, and identified a total of 15 relevant influencing factors. These factors exerted differential effects on player mobility between starter and substitute positions at the beginning of a new season and during the season. The 15 factors were further grouped into three domains: Ability-related Factors, Social Factors, and Opportunities. Interview data indicate that, owing to the Matthew Effect, starters are not easily displaced by substitutes: players who hold an initial starting advantage are granted more opportunities, which fosters the development of stronger football-specific competencies and thereby consolidates their starting roles. To mitigate this dynamic, the study identified four approaches to counteract the Matthew Effect-Physical Development, Learning from the Sidelines, Individualized Training, and Trust Building. These findings extend the application of Social Stratification Theory to competitive sport and address how the Matthew Effect can be effectively mitigated in that context. Accordingly, the results possess both theoretical significance and important practical implications.

title: The Evolution and Diversification of Stock-Flow Consistent Modelling: A Bibliometric Review
affiliations: Universidad Central del Ecuador, Students, Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales (FLACSO) - Ecuador, Students,  and Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales (FLACSO) - Ecuador, Students

detail.title: The Evolution and Diversification of Stock-Flow Consistent Modelling: A Bibliometric Review
detail.abstract: This paper presents a bibliometric analysis of the Stock-Flow Consistent (SFC) literature from 1975 to 2026. The corpus includes 479 publications from Scopus, Web of Science, and expert-guided screening. Building on the classification proposed by Nikiforos and Zezza (2017), using keyword-based classification and manual validation, the paper maps the evolution of five major research areas: extensions of the core SFC framework, open-economy models, empirical SFC models, ecological SFC models, and SFC-agent–based models. The results show a clear expansion of the literature after the Global Financial Crisis, followed by further acceleration after 2017. Recent growth is especially visible in empirical and ecological SFC applications, as well as in works combining multiple research areas. The journal mapping also shows that, while SFC research remains strongly rooted in heterodox economics outlets, it has increasingly expanded into interdisciplinary and non-traditional journals. The paper contributes by updating the 2017 survey and documenting the diversification and broader diffusion of SFC research.

title: Climate Change and Education: Evidence from Palestine
affiliations: and Levy Economics Institute of Bard College

detail.title: Climate Change and Education: Evidence from Palestine
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of climate change on women’s education in Palestine, focusing on how climatic factors affect years of schooling. Using pooled data from the Palestinian Labor Force Survey and climate indicators from the Palestinian Meteorological Department, the analysis explores both immediate and lagged effects of climate change on women’s years of schooling. Findings reveal gendered disparities in the effects of rainfall and temperature on schooling, with women facing unique vulnerabilities. Mechanism analysis indicates that agricultural households in Palestine are highly vulnerable to climatic shocks which in turn increases the vulnerability of girls in these households; Climatic shocks negatively impact farming productivity and the overall working environment, exacerbating the challenges faced by these families. The study also identifies regional heterogeneities, with southern districts showing greater resilience compared to central and northern regions, while Jericho faces pronounced adverse impacts.

title: The Paradox of Strategic Altruism
affiliations: University of Southampton - Faculty of Economic, Social and Political Sciences, University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS) and University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS)

detail.title: The Paradox of Strategic Altruism
detail.abstract: Can altruism serve as the behavioral foundation for efficient institutional design? We study full implementation in Berge equilibrium, the solution concept that formalizes strategic altruism: each agent's opponents collectively maximize her payoff. While Berge equilibrium resolves the Prisoner's Dilemma and can eliminate cooperation failures in social dilemmas, we show that this optimism does not survive the move from individual behavior to institutional design. First, we show that the weak Pareto optimal rule is not implementable in Berge equilibrium. Second, on the unrestricted domain of strict preferences, any social choice rule that is both weakly Pareto efficient and implementable in Berge equilibrium must be dictatorial. Finally, we show that Berge implementability is strictly more demanding than Nash implementability: every social goal achievable under strategic altruism is also achievable under self-interest, but not vice versa. The very feature that makes Berge equilibrium appealing at the behavioral level, that is, opponents protecting each agent's payoff, is precisely what forecloses efficient, non-dictatorial institutions at the design level.

title: Hurdle Rates and Canada's State-Capacity Challenge in the Age of Machine Knowledge Capital

detail.title: Hurdle Rates and Canada's State-Capacity Challenge in the Age of Machine Knowledge Capital

contentType.other: Notes for Remarks at a roundtable

detail.abstract: This note reframes Canada's state-capacity challenge in the era of machine knowledge capital as a problem of heterogeneous hurdle rates. Accelerating technological change, geopolitical uncertainty, large sunk costs and winner-take-most dynamics raise the option value of waiting, while investors differ in their ability to bear risk and capture indirect returns. Large state-led economies and jurisdictions with deep pools of private capital can therefore undertake investments that small open economies cannot. For Canada, the appropriate policy response is not indiscriminate subsidization, but establishing the institutional capacity to identify projects which are sidelined by excessively high hurdle rates for private capital of modest scale, yet make sense at the societal level, and to act on these projects. This requires disciplined project evaluation, public equity and retention mechanisms, and technically capable teams able to structure and implement complex investments.

title: Understanding the Investment Behaviour of Gen Z
affiliations: , Mata Sundri College For Women, Graphic Era Hill University and Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee University

detail.title: Understanding the Investment Behaviour of Gen Z
detail.abstract: Gen-Z is one of the most affected generations because of pandemics, economic uncertainties and geo-political challenges. But a generation with much familiarity and access to the internet and smartphones makes it more interesting to study how they invest and their investment preferences. This study aims to highlight how Gen-Z prefers to invest and if they don't invest what's stopping them from investing.

title: Optimal Selling of Defaultable Assets using the Distribution Builder
affiliations: and Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Optimal Selling of Defaultable Assets using the Distribution Builder
detail.abstract: We consider the problem of when it is best to sell a risky asset in the framework of the distribution builder approach under the consideration of potential ruin. This approach allows investors to express their preferences directly as a desired target distribution without first specifying a risk aversion or utility function. Mathematically, the problem is closely related to the Skorokhod embedding problem, where the goal is to attain a given distribution by stopping a diffusion process. We work in a general framework of one-dimensional diffusion processes and extend existing results to include the possibility of ruin. We first provide a full characterization of the set of distributions that can be attained before ruin occurs. Then, we formulate two optimization problems that tackle the issue of what to do if the originally specified distribution is either not attainable or not optimal: finding the attainable distribution closest to an unattainable distribution and selecting an optimal attainable distribution under first-order stochastic dominance constraints if the originally specified distribution is attainable, but not optimal. We show existence and uniqueness of solutions to these constrained convex optimization problems in an extended f-divergence framework, provide an analytic characterization of solutions and give numerical examples.

title: Extending Safety Performance Functions with Connected Vehicle Data Using a Random-Parameter Negative Binomial Lindley Model with Spatial Effect
affiliations: University of Central Florida, University of Central Florida, University of Central Florida and University of Central Florida

detail.title: Extending Safety Performance Functions with Connected Vehicle Data Using a Random-Parameter Negative Binomial Lindley Model with Spatial Effect
detail.abstract: Severe crashes remain a critical roadway safety concern, yet traditional Safety Performance Functions (SPFs) primarily rely on traffic exposure and roadway characteristics, often overlooking driving behavior. Leveraging high-resolution connected vehicle (CV) trajectory data, this study derives behavioral measures including hard braking, hard acceleration, radial acceleration, lane changes, operating speeds, and speed variability, and integrates them into an extended SPF framework for segment-level crash frequency modeling. Using data from the Lake–Sumter MPO region in Florida, Bayesian Random Parameter Negative Binomial-Lindley models with spatial effects are estimated separately for two-lane and multilane roadway segments for both severe (KA) and total (KABCO) crashes to account for unobserved heterogeneity and spatial dependence among roadway segments. Results indicate that CV-based behavioral variables significantly improve model fit and predictive performance compared to traditional SPFs. Among the driving behavior variables, the proportion of radial acceleration on two-lane segments and the proportion of lane changes on multilane segments are positively associated with higher KA and KABCO crash frequencies, respectively. From the elasticity analysis, traffic volume (AADT) is identified as the most influential factor across facilities, while over speeding proportion (0-10%) and speed standard deviation show strong effects for two-lane KA and KABCO crashes, respectively, and speed standard deviation remains particularly influential for multilane KABCO crashes. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach for capturing behavioral risk factors at the network level and offers practical insights for proactive safety management and prioritization. By integrating CV data into SPF modeling, this study advances behavior-informed, data-driven roadway safety analysis.

title: Causal Analysis of Road Segment Crashes Using Doubly Robust Estimation
affiliations: Cleveland State University, Cleveland State University, Cleveland State University, University of Central Florida, University of Central Florida and Cleveland State University

detail.title: Causal Analysis of Road Segment Crashes Using Doubly Robust Estimation
detail.abstract: Inadequate roadway infrastructure design can contribute to crash occurrence. Conventional crash-frequency models do not identify causal effects, leaving individual design elements confounded by traffic volume, facility type, and other exposure variables. This study estimates the causal effects of seven roadway infrastructure and operational characteristics traffic volume (AADT), segment length, median width, number of lanes, traffic signal density, posted speed limit, and bike-lane presence on segment-level crash counts across 1,818 segments in Orlando, Florida. We implement a doubly robust augmented inverse probability weighting (DR-AIPW) estimator combining hypothesis-specific propensity-score models with a zero-inflated negative binomial generalized additive outcome model, reporting the average treatment effect (ATE), the effect on the treated (ATT), and the overlap-weighted effect (ATO) with 2,000 bootstrap replications. Traffic volume and segment length show the largest, most consistent effects: crossing ~36,000 vpd raises expected crashes by 1.61 (ATO; p = 0.004), and exceeding ~270 ft by 2.51 (ATE; p < 0.001; +81%). Signal density shows a strong negative association (ATO = −2.79, ~90% below the mean; p < 0.001), reflecting crash allocation between intersections and segments rather than a causal benefit. Number of lanes and median width show no independent effect once exposure is controlled. The posted-limit effect is significant on average (ATE = +1.91) but null within the overlap region (ATO = +0.04; p = 0.916). Bike-lane presence reduces crashes only where installed (ATT = −2.03, a 65% reduction; p = 0.009). Estimand divergence localizes where effects are causally supported versus overlap-driven.

title: Water Scarcity Management and Housing Markets: Evidence from Water Impact Fees in Colorado

detail.title: Water Scarcity Management and Housing Markets: Evidence from Water Impact Fees in Colorado
detail.abstract: This paper studies local water scarcity management policies designed to align privately- and socially-optimal construction of new housing. Using the staggered adoption of water impact fee policies that scale homebuilder fees by expected water use, I find that these variable fees reduce new single-family lot sizes and irrigated areas, decreasing household water use and altering the market's hedonic equilibrium pricing. I then incorporate these builder incentives into an equilibrium model of the housing market. Variable impact fees increase welfare but capture a small share of the welfare gains and water savings compared to first-best corrective water rates.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Financial Literacy, and Sustainable Investment Behaviour: An Integrated Model of Young Investors in India

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Financial Literacy, and Sustainable Investment Behaviour: An Integrated Model of Young Investors in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants prior to completing the online survey. The data collection protocol ensured participant anonymity, voluntary participation, and confidentiality of all responses. Institutional review/ethics committee approval was obtained from the author's institution prior to study commencement.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study develops and empirically tests an integrated model examining how Artificial Intelligence (AI) awareness, digital financial literacy, perceived usefulness, and trust influence sustainable investment intention among young investors in India, with Financial Self-Efficacy as mediator and ESG Awareness as moderator. Using primary data from 527 young investors (age 18-35) collected via online survey, we employ SmartPLS 4 to test the proposed model using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Key findings: (1) AI Awareness significantly predicts Perceived Usefulness (β=0.487, p<0.001) and Sustainable Investment Intention (β=0.234, p<0.001); (2) Digital Financial Literacy strongly predicts Perceived Usefulness (β=0.562, p<0.001) and Intention (β=0.328, p<0.001); (3) Trust moderates the relationship between Perceived Usefulness and Intention (β_interaction=0.189, p<0.01), with stronger effects at high trust levels; (4) Financial Self-Efficacy fully mediates the AI Awareness → Intention relationship (indirect effect=0.156, 95% CI: [0.089, 0.243]); (5) ESG Awareness amplifies Digital Literacy's effect on Intention (β_moderation=0.267, p<0.001); (6) Multi-group analysis reveals gender differences (female investors show stronger ESG preference, β_diff=0.213, p<0.01) and income-level differences (high-income investors more responsive to Trust). Model explains 68.4% of Sustainable Investment Intention variance (R²=0.684). Study contributes to behavioral finance and sustainable investment literature by: (1) examining AI's role in investment decisions among emerging market youth, (2) integrating digital literacy, trust, and self-efficacy in single model, (3) identifying gender and income-based segments for targeted financial inclusion. Findings have implications for fintech platforms, financial advisors, and regulators in India promoting sustainable investment among young investors.

title: The Unmatched Deduction: Labor Substitution, Cloud Transactions, and the Information Architecture of the Tax Code

detail.title: The Unmatched Deduction: Labor Substitution, Cloud Transactions, and the Information Architecture of the Tax Code
detail.abstract: American tax administration rests on third-party reporting: one person pays another, the payer files an information return, and the Internal Revenue Service checks that return against the payee's own. The same records do a second and less examined job. The Government Accountability Office found in 1993 that a business wage deduction could be corroborated by comparing it against the employer's own wage and employment tax filings, and that the other major categories could not be corroborated as readily: service payments to corporations and bad debts would require information returns that did not exist, while pensions, rents and interest faced data and systems limitations. Wages were the major business deduction most readily susceptible to the operation under the system as it stood. The two jobs differ: relative to the employee the wage statement is a third-party report, while relative to the employer it is a separately filed collateral record supporting a cross-form consistency check. This Article identifies a business input with neither, and names it the unmatched deduction: a deduction, or set of deductions, that displaces a wage expense corroborable in that way and is accompanied by no analogous standardized collateral filing. It traces a descent from the wage, through the purchased cloud service, which generates no transaction-level return because of the corporate-payee exemption, to internal deployment, which generates no payment corresponding to the function performed. Firms have shifted expenditure between payroll and capital for as long as both categories have existed; what is new is the breadth of work a reconfigurable computing substrate can move at once. The Article shows that the 2025 cloud transaction regulations, the Code's first dedicated transactional vocabulary for on-demand computing, could not reach internally deployed compute on any extension, because a transaction requires a counterparty. It concludes that provider reporting can supply genuine counterparty verification for purchased compute, exceeding what the wage deduction ever had, while a first party schedule can restore only cross-form visibility for the internal case, where no independent party exists to stand behind either side of a match.

title:
The Lead Zero Standard 

A Governance Protocol for Clinician-As-Originator Architecture in Ai-Assisted Medicine, Version 3.0
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
The Lead Zero Standard 

A Governance Protocol for Clinician-As-Originator Architecture in Ai-Assisted Medicine, Version 3.0

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Dr. Enam Satti is the Founder of AegisMD and the author of its Clinical AI Red Teaming Framework, an open specification protocol for clinical AI safety evaluation from which the 34 adversarial attack classes documented in this standard originated. The governance framework proposed in this manuscript, if adopted, could benefit organizations providing clinical AI safety and red teaming services, including AegisMD. Dr. Satti asserts that this submission is motivated exclusively by patient safety and physician accountability. The Lead Zero Standard is published as an open specification, freely available to all implementers without licensing restriction or commercial obligation. As of the date of this publication, AegisMD has no clients, has conducted no commercial evaluations, and has generated no revenue. The author has received no financial benefit of any kind from AegisMD to date.

publicationDetails.detailsText: No, this paper has not been published anywhere before, it has no existing DOI, this is an original submission.

detail.abstract:
Background
The prevailing human-in-the-loop governance model for clinical AI positions the clinician as a secondary auditor of AI-generated suggestions rather than the primary architect of clinical care. This creates a critical accountability asymmetry and exposes patient populations globally to geographical algorithmic bias. In January 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration codified this model by exempting clinical decision support software from premarket review, provided a clinician can independently review the output. Version 2.0 of the Lead Zero Standard, published on SSRN on May 4, 2026, established the Clinician-as-Originator principle and the 0-1-0 cycle as the foundational governance architecture for clinical AI in individual patient care. Public stress testing following publication identified architectural gaps requiring formal resolution.

Purpose
Version 3.0 strengthens the V2 architecture through six foundational additions: the Admissibility Layer, the Commit Boundary, Tier-Dependent Decision Provenance, Low-Resource and Low-Literacy Deployment Sovereignty, Semantic Drift Behavioral Benchmarking, and Minimum Architectural Requirements. Building on this foundation, Version 3.0 further establishes that clinical authority is not adequately governed as a one-time declaration at the point of intent. It must remain continuously valid through to the point of execution. This distinction, between authority persistence and authority validity, is operationalized through Continuous Authority Validity monitoring, an Output Completeness Verification requirement for compressed clinical outputs, physiologically grounded definitions of irreversibility at the Commit Boundary, a formal Systemic Error State protocol, explicit governance requirements for agentic and multi-component AI architectures, and explicit patient sovereignty protections. The adversarial testing framework was expanded from 24 to 34 verified attack classes across four categories, independently stress-tested against both human governance review and adversarial AI red-teaming.

Scope
Version 3.0 maintains the V2 scope. Adult individual patient care. Pediatric and obstetric extensions remain reserved for future versions.

Status
This is a working paper. It has not been prospectively validated through clinical implementation. Pilot deployment studies are needed.

title: Machine Learning Applications in Demand Forecasting for Supply Chain Management: A Systematic Literature Review

detail.title: Machine Learning Applications in Demand Forecasting for Supply Chain Management: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: Accurate demand forecasting remains a persistent challenge in supply chain management, with poor predictions contributing to bullwhip effects and operational inefficiencies. While machine learning (ML) is increasingly applied to address this challenge, a holistic review focused specifically on ML algorithms for demand forecasting has been lacking. This report conducts a systematic literature review, following Kitchenham and Charters' guidelines and the PRISMA framework, of 27 academic studies and 8 industry reports examining ML applications in demand forecasting across supply chains. The reviewed studies collectively employ 26 distinct ML techniques, spanning traditional machine learning, deep learning, ensemble methods, and hybrid models, across 18 industry sectors consolidated into five broad categories. Findings show that Retail & Consumer Markets (48%) and Manufacturing & Industrial (30%) sectors dominate current research, with deep learning (33%) and traditional ML (30%) as the most common approaches. Improved forecast accuracy over traditional statistical models emerged as the most frequently cited benefit (37% of studies), alongside gains in handling volatile demand, scalability across large SKU portfolios, and real-time prediction capability. Real-world industry applications, including Coles' AI-enabled fulfilment centers in Australia, illustrate practical adoption but often lack empirical validation or benchmarking depth. Recurring limitations across the literature include small or limited datasets, constrained model scalability, poor generalizability across industries and geographies, and trade-offs between interpretability and model complexity. The review identifies key research gaps, including the need for multi-objective forecasting, cross-domain transfer learning, improved uncertainty quantification, and stronger human-AI collaboration. These findings suggest that while ML offers substantial and industry-tailored improvements in forecasting accuracy and responsiveness, realizing its full potential requires standardized benchmarking, interdisciplinary research, and closer alignment between ML deployment and organizational data infrastructure and readiness.

title: Educating All Retail Investors in a Billion-Euro Market
affiliations: University of Kiel - Institute for Quantitative Business and Economics Research (QBER) and University of Kiel - Institute for Quantitative Business and Economics Research (QBER)

detail.title: Educating All Retail Investors in a Billion-Euro Market
detail.abstract: The German regulator Bafin designed an educational intervention that targets investors trading billions and losing millions in the market for retail structured products. We estimate that the intervention reduces retail losses by 340 million euros per year.

title:
Signed-Event Learning and Adaptive Utility:
 A Minimal Model of Endogenous Preferences -Identification, Endogenous Cycles, and First Measurements
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Signed-Event Learning and Adaptive Utility:
 A Minimal Model of Endogenous Preferences -Identification, Endogenous Cycles, and First Measurements
detail.abstract: We propose a minimal learning model in which individuals encode personally realized gains and losses (events E) into action weights W, with learning sensitivity S governing the size and learning period T the timing of updates; W enters choice values as a learned multiplier on baseline utility, V = U⁰•e^W-C, and thereby constitutes utility, expectations, and behavior. The agent-side primitives are domain-general; finance serves as the first closed environment because events, feedback, and data are sharpest there. Events are defined at the Core level as signed reinforcement signals attributed to actions, and are operationally narrowed to realized material returns in the finance application. Fixing the error-correction skeleton W ← W + L•S•(e-W) yields three identification results: macro means identify only S/T; the stationary cross-sectional variance Sσ²/(2-S) identifies S while the excess kurtosis of one-period changes, exactly 3(T-1), identifies T; and learning and forgetting speeds are locked, to leading order in S, into the single rate S/T. Closing the price-feedback loop produces a bubble phase boundary without social imitation, and adding a single environmental anchor α generates endogenous boom-bust cycles through a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation (a Hopf bifurcation in the continuous-time mean-field limit) with onset period P = 2π/√(α•S/T). Inverting this law, we calibrate the model to the 16-year financial cycle (BIS) and to a directly measured scar half-life: in event-quiet windows of Gallup's U.S. stock-ownership series (1998-2025) we estimate a leakage rate of 0.047-0.084 per year (half-life 8-15 years), and an eight-year participation plateau amid a tripling market is difficult to reconcile with a pure common-price-signal benchmark and is consistent with the personal signed-event channel. Korean Securities Depository ownership data (2019-2025) show an entry surge persisting through the 2022 bear market, consistent with the model's entry-exit asymmetry prediction. The contribution is compression, not coverage; an explicit list of falsification conditions is provided.

title: Beyond the Coupon: Climate Risk and the Quantity-Maturity Design of Chinese Interbank Bonds

detail.title: Beyond the Coupon: Climate Risk and the Quantity-Maturity Design of Chinese Interbank Bonds
detail.abstract: This paper studies two financing terms that coupon regressions leave aside: how much an issuer places and how long it borrows. The data cover 1,468 Chinese interbank medium-term notes from 165 listed legal issuers over 2010-2025. I measure climate exposure in three ways-weather at the registered location, national ETS coverage matched by legal entity and date, and climate-risk language in the latest available annual report-and estimate issuer and issue-month fixed-effects models. None of the nine main coefficients survives issuer-clustered wild-bootstrap inference and multiplicity correction. The nulls are not equally informative: equivalence tests rule out effects beyond ±10% only for the language measure in the issue-size and maturity equations. Most remaining intervals are too wide for such a conclusion, and ETS estimates draw on changes among only 17 transaction-level issuers. In the annual panel, issuance rises before firms enter ETS scope as well as afterward. That lead pattern rules out a causal policy interpretation. Overall, the evidence sets limits on what the current measures and sample can establish; it does not show that climate risk is absent from financing decisions.

title: The Services That Pay for Cash Transfers to Women: Evidence from Indian State Budgets
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Services That Pay for Cash Transfers to Women: Evidence from Indian State Budgets
detail.abstract: Twelve Indian states pay unconditional monthly cash transfers to adult women. The 2025-26 provisions total US$19 billion, reaching about 95 million women, making this one of the largest subnational women-targeted cash transfer expansions in the world. These states face centrally enforced borrowing ceilings and heavy salary commitments, so much of the cost falls on other spending. In a validated panel of nineteen states' budgeted spending from 2015-16 to 2026-27, compared across sectors within the same state and year, the displacement follows one measured rule: the larger the central government's co-funding share in a sector, the more state money leaves it, while central releases to that sector hold steady. Salary shares, women's time use, and official gender-budget classifications add nothing once co-funding is controlled. The result survives randomization and wild-bootstrap inference, pre-treatment measurement, drop-one-sector tests, and re-estimation on audited accounts. What a transfer costs in public services depends on which of those services an upper tier of government co-funds. Because the most co-funded sectors are water supply, nutrition, and family welfare, the incidence falls on the services that substitute for women's unpaid work.

title: Supramarginal Versus Gross Total Resection in Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma: A Post-hoc Pooled Individual-Participant Analysis of Two Randomised Surgical Trials
affiliations: University of Toronto - Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, University of Gothenburg - Sahlgrenska University Hospital, University of Turku - Division of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Southern Denmark, Medical University of Vienna - Department of Neurosurgery and Pennsylvania State University - Penn State Hershey Medical Center

detail.title: Supramarginal Versus Gross Total Resection in Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma: A Post-hoc Pooled Individual-Participant Analysis of Two Randomised Surgical Trials

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Each trial received ethics approval from the responsible national, regional, or institutional committee, and all participants provided written informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Norwegian Cancer Society, and Nordic Cancer Union.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: We did a post-hoc pooled individual-participant analysis of G-SUMIT and the European trial at four Canadian and 12 European academic neurosurgery centres. The trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04737577 and NCT04243005

detail.abstract:
Background: Resection beyond the contrast-enhancing margin could remove infiltrating glioblastoma but might increase neurological risk. Retrospective comparisons suggest benefit but are vulnerable to anatomical and prognostic selection bias. We assessed pooled randomised evidence comparing supramarginal resection (SMR) with gross total resection (GTR).

Methods: We did a post-hoc pooled individual-participant analysis of G-SUMIT and the European trial at four Canadian and 12 European academic neurosurgery centres. Adults with anatomically favourable presumed high-grade glioma or glioblastoma were randomly assigned (1:1) to GTR or SMR. The primary cohort comprised 67 patients with histopathologically confirmed glioblastoma. Outcomes were overall and progression-free survival. Cox models adjusted for age, Karnofsky performance status, and trial; Bayesian analyses estimated posterior probabilities of benefit. The trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04737577 and NCT04243005.

Findings: Between July 1, 2020, and June 30, 2025, 82 patients were randomised; 67 entered the primary cohort (33 GTR and 34 SMR). Median follow-up was 23·6 months. There were 25 deaths and 39 progression-free survival events. For SMR versus GTR, unadjusted hazard ratios were 1·08 (95% CI 0·49–2·38) for death and 0·67 (0·36–1·27) for progression or death; adjusted hazard ratios were 0·79 (0·33–1·89) and 0·43 (0·21–0·87), respectively. Under the data-informed prior, posterior probabilities of benefit were 0·83 for death and 0·97 for progression or death. New neurological deficits occurred in three of 33 patients (9%) assigned to GTR and four of 32 (13%) assigned to SMR; no deaths occurred within 30 days.Interpretation SMR was feasible and associated with a lower adjusted hazard of progression or death; overall-survival benefit was not established. These findings support a definitive event-driven trial but not routine adoption of SMR. Funding: Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Norwegian Cancer Society, and Nordic Cancer Union.

title: Optimal Grading: A Unified Approach
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Optimal Grading: A Unified Approach
detail.abstract: We develop a unified approach to optimal grading in an all-pay contest in which a designer assigns a fixed vector of heterogeneous prizes to maximize expected total effort. The approach covers two information regimes and identifies a common principle: iron locally misordered incentive returns and assign prizes assortatively across the resulting grades. Under rank-only grading, assignments depend only on ordinal ranks. Ironing cumulative rank coefficients-via the least concave majorant or the pool-adjacentviolators algorithm-determines which adjacent ranks are pooled and which prizes are randomized within each grade. Under performance-contingent grading, assignments may depend on numerical effort. The optimum irons virtual ability, forms endogenous type grades, and assigns prize blocks assortatively across grades. A failing grade below a minimum passing effort and a collection of effort brackets implement the direct optimum while preserving full prize assignment.

title: Knowing Who to Lend To - What the Accounts and Filings of Ten Digital Banks in Five Markets Show About Why Some of Them Reach Profit and Others Do Not

detail.title: Knowing Who to Lend To - What the Accounts and Filings of Ten Digital Banks in Five Markets Show About Why Some of Them Reach Profit and Others Do Not

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author participated in the Nafis Leadership Programme, Cohort III, organised by the Emirati Talent Competitiveness Council in partnership with the UAE Government Leaders Program. The Korea immersion within that programme was delivered by the National University of Singapore Business School Executive Education. The challenger bank counts that open this paper were first encountered in a session on that immersion. Jungkiu Choi, who taught that session, subsequently provided peer review of this paper across four rounds; he is acknowledged accordingly and received no compensation. The author visited KakaoBank in Pangyo as a guest of that programme in July 2026 and met members of its management. He is a national of the United Arab Emirates, one of the markets examined. No funding was received for this research. The author holds no financial interest in any institution examined.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, patients, or personal data. It is based entirely on published financial statements, regulatory disclosures and supervisory records. No ethics approval was required. A site visit to one institution took place during a leadership programme and is declared as an interest; no data from that visit is used in the paper.

detail.abstract:
Boston Consulting Group, the management consultancy, counts 92 profitable challenger banks worldwide out of roughly 650, up from 23 of 453 two years earlier. Profitability is arriving in the sector; scale is not. This paper asks what separates the banks reaching profit from those that have not, reading the accounts, regulatory filings and supervisory records of ten digital banks across Singapore, Korea, Australia, the United Arab Emirates and Brazil for 2024 and 2025.

There is a survival threshold, illustrated by the Australian failures of 2020 to 2022, but it sits on earning assets rather than on lending: a bank holding deposits against nothing does not survive, while one holding securities and earning fees can lend almost nothing and prosper. The loan-to-deposit ratio, the measure usually applied, is a proxy for that threshold which stops working once a bank earns from anything else, and above the floor it no longer orders outcomes at all, though it continues to bear on them through funding cost.

What separates the banks already lending is the annual credit charge. Measured against the average loan book it runs from 0.51 per cent to 12.6 across the nine for which it is comparable, and in Singapore the two lowest belong to the only two banks at or near profit. That ordering holds within a market. It does not travel across pricing environments: Nubank, the largest challenger bank in the world, runs a credit charge near nine per cent and a return on equity of 33, because Brazilian yields carry it. A charge is half a sentence, and the yield is the other half.

Across two years four of the five reduced that charge and one did not. Whether those movements reflect improving judgement or losses not yet recognised on rapidly growing books cannot be settled from a ratio alone. The paper attempts a correction from disclosures banks already publish under IFRS 9, using opening balances, origination volumes and the coverage held against loans that have deteriorated but not yet defaulted, and sets out how far that gets. Five objections are put to the finding and tested against the same accounts, among them the cost-to-income ratio conventionally used in its place, and the collateral behind the lowest charges.

The pattern follows where each bank's credit judgement comes from. It can be bought, built, or borrowed from a position where transactions and repayments are already visible. Which source a bank draws on, and how far through it the bank has progressed, explains more about its trajectory than either its distribution or its deployment ratio. K bank marks the boundary: a low charge on the asset side, on a book more than half of which carries collateral or a guarantee, and a profit that fell anyway because its funding cost moved against it.

Three patterns appear only when the five markets are read together. These banks are acquiring collateral rather than moving further from it, in three markets at once. Defaults in their books leave by write-off rather than by cure. And the share of a year's charge resting on lending originated within it tracks how fast a bank is growing rather than where it operates.

Two years is the whole of the record these banks have. The paper sets out what that permits and what it does not.

title: Robust Scientific AI Agents Under Noisy, Data-Scarce Conditions: Adaptive Model Selection, Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning, and Noise-Robust Surrogate Learning

detail.title: Robust Scientific AI Agents Under Noisy, Data-Scarce Conditions: Adaptive Model Selection, Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning, and Noise-Robust Surrogate Learning
detail.abstract: Scientific AI systems are increasingly expected to reason over scarce observations, noisy measurements, unstable simulators, and heterogeneous model families. Existing work usually treats these difficulties separately: robust surrogate models address noisy regression, routing systems select among language models, and control-theoretic allocation methods adapt traffic under non-stationary workloads. This paper argues that noisy, data-scarce scientific workflows require an integrated agent architecture rather than a single fixed predictor. We introduce Robust Scientific AI Agents (RSA-Agents), a framework that represents scientific problem solving as a closed-loop decision process over candidate surrogate models, symbolic tools, validation signals, uncertainty estimates, and execution constraints. The agent maintains a portfolio of candidate scientific models, estimates their task-conditioned reliability from limited evidence, and allocates future calls through a validation-weighted selection rule with persistent exploration. Noise-robust models such as ER-KAN provide the agent with a safer surrogate option when clean-data accuracy is misleading, while adaptive routing and feedback-control principles prevent static model commitments under regime change. In a synthetic pilot benchmark spanning eight analytic functions, three data budgets, and three noise levels, a validation-weighted RSA-Agent reduces mean squared error by 7.7% relative to the best static surrogate overall and by 27.7% in the high-noise setting, while underperforming on clean regimes. These results support the central thesis: robust scientific AI should be evaluated as an adaptive agentic system under uncertainty, not only as a collection of isolated predictors.

title: Equivalence Testing for Risk-Compute Engines Beyond Terminal Metrics: Path Functionals and Attribution Summaries
affiliations: Association for Financial Professionals (AFP)

detail.title: Equivalence Testing for Risk-Compute Engines Beyond Terminal Metrics: Path Functionals and Attribution Summaries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and chief executive officer of Scientific Analytics Alliance Inc., which develops the software harness under test in this paper. To mitigate this interest, all acceptance thresholds were declared before execution and all inputs, code revisions, and outputs are sealed under SHA-256 digests published with the paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is computational research involving no human participants, patients, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as internal research of Scientific Analytics Alliance Inc.

detail.abstract: Institutional risk controls consume more than terminal loss quantiles: investment mandates cap maximum drawdown, committee reporting tracks time underwater and recovery, and remediation decisions are ranked by attribution. Validation practice, however, concentrates on terminal metrics. This paper extends a pre-declared equivalence-testing protocol for risk-compute engines from terminal tail metrics to two further object classes: path functionals (maximum drawdown, time underwater, recovery completion day, jump count) and attribution summaries (portfolio loss, gross attribution, top-family share, attribution concentration). The protocol compares a deterministic low-discrepancy stream against a seeded pseudo-random Monte Carlo reference at 10,000,000 paths per method under acceptance thresholds declared before execution. As instantiated, it is a pre-declared tolerance benchmark rather than a formal inferential equivalence test; the distinction, and the migration path to confidence-bounded margins, are stated explicitly. Two design contributions arise. First, a two-standard split: deterministically replayed quantities (published stress rows) are held to numerical exactness at an absolute tolerance of 10-9 , while sampled quantities are held to sampling-scale agreement; mixing the two standards would weaken both. Second, an explicit treatment of integer-valued functionals, whose quantile agreement presents as exact zeros at scale; we argue these are quantization effects, not anomalies-and, conversely, not evidence of distribution-level identity. Across 180 pre-declared checks-96 path-functional rows, 24 terminal-metric cross-check rows, 12 exact stress-replay integrity rows, and 48 stochastic attribution-summary rows-every check passes, with minimum headroom of 1.67× over threshold. The largest gaps concentrate in the empirical-bootstrap family, where inversion of a coarse 199-observation empirical distribution function, not the sampler, drives the difference. All inputs, code revisions, and outputs are sealed under SHA-256 digests, runs are CPU-only with bounded memory, and each experiment is reproducible from two commands when executed against the sealed artifact packs.

title: Encoding Purpose: Logic Model Dynamics of PONs' Process, Activities, Outputs, and Outcomes
affiliations: , , , University of Illinois Chicago, Northwestern University, University of Illinois at Chicago and Northwestern University

detail.title: Encoding Purpose: Logic Model Dynamics of PONs' Process, Activities, Outputs, and Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No data collection and thus no ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: There is no funding.

detail.abstract: The increasing complexity of public issues has led to a rise in purpose-oriented networks (PONs). These networks are bounded, self-referential collaborations among independent actors sharing a common public purpose. This systematic review explores how empirical research worldwide conceptualizes and links processes, activities, outputs, and outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, the review analyzes 3,488 articles and, after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, selects 205 for review. Using Agranoff and McGuire's (2001) framework to identify network processes, the study finds that mobilizing and synthesizing are the most commonly observed in the literature. Conversely, activating and framing are less frequent, indicating a limited understanding of how networks create meaning and structure participation over time. Studies rarely specify the activities that link processes to results. Outputs and outcomes are inconsistently defined, often emphasizing network-level products over community or organizational results. Important features like age and size are also rarely reported. The primary contribution of this review is to clarify how research on PONs describes these connections, highlight methodological and conceptual gaps, and offer a checklist to guide future research.

title: Auditing Anonymized Tick Data: A Bias-Robust Framework for Detecting Affine Scaling and Directional Inversion in Intraday Markets

detail.title: Auditing Anonymized Tick Data: A Bias-Robust Framework for Detecting Affine Scaling and Directional Inversion in Intraday Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest Statement The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently and received no funding from any institution, firm, or individual. No financial relationships exist with any organization that could have an interest in the submitted work. The NSE intraday data used in the empirical analysis was collected by the author through a licensed Upstox API connection for independent research purposes. The author provides independent quantitative data audit services; no client data was used in this paper.

detail.abstract: When quantitative firms share proprietary tick data with external auditors under NDA, they routinely apply sanitizing transformations-principally affine price scaling (P′ = αP + β) and directional inversion (P′ =-P + C)-to prevent alpha leakage. Standard audit pipelines, calibrated for exchange-native tick sizes and expecting the classical negative leverage effect, fail silently under both transformations. We make three contributions. First, we show that the tick size of an affine-scaled series can be recovered exactly via the greatest common divisor (GCD) of absolute price movements, bypassing the scaling constant entirely. Second, we apply the leverage-effect puzzle of Aït-Sahalia, Fan and Li (2011) to the inversion-detection problem, demonstrating that at 1-minute frequency the standard lagged correlation estimator produces near-zero or reversed signals on all markets-not merely on Indian equity as sometimes claimed-making leveragebased detectors unreliable. Third, we show that the order-book bid-ask constraint (Ask > Bid) is violated in 100% of rows after inversion when Level-2 data is available, providing a definitive, bias-free test. We validate all three results on 22,419 one-minute bars across 12 NSE large-cap symbols and release the detection framework as open auditing infrastructure.

title:
Working paper: Self-regularizing Generalized Linear Models: 
Assumption-Lean Estimation and Prediction under Ill-Conditioning

detail.title:
Working paper: Self-regularizing Generalized Linear Models: 
Assumption-Lean Estimation and Prediction under Ill-Conditioning
detail.abstract: We introduce self-regularizing generalized linear models for reliable inference and prediction under severe ill-conditioning and rank deficiency, without specifying a response distribution or variance function. A unique Critical Parameter enables assumption-lean coefficient inference, while vanishing complexity regularization provides stable prediction with predictive performance comparable to or better than cross-validated regularization in a single fit. The framework combines interpretable inference with fast, low-cost regularized prediction.

title: Cheapflation Cycles

detail.title: Cheapflation Cycles
detail.abstract: We document a new source of fluctuations in inflation inequality. When the cost of upstream inputs rises, varieties within a product category tend to have similar absolute price increases. However, the same absolute price increase constitutes a larger percentage change for low-price products, resulting in excess inflation at the low end ("cheapflation"). Since low-income households tend to buy lower-priced varieties, the inflation rates they face are disproportionately sensitive to upstream costs. Using data on food-at-home purchases, we show that this mechanism generates cycles in inflation inequality and excess volatility in inflation for low-income households relative to high-income households. This channel parsimoniously accounts for observed fluctuations in inflation inequality over time, including surges in cheapflation and inflation inequality during both the Great Recession and the 2021--2023 inflation surge. Income-group price indices constructed from public inflation statistics mask these within-category differences in inflation and thus understate the excess cost-sensitivity and volatility of inflation for low-income households. We provide suggestive evidence that this mechanism applies to categories beyond food at home. The same mechanism also leads to systematic differences in inflation across cities and import price inflation across countries in response to nationwide and global cost shocks.

title:
Beyond the 2030 Agenda: 
Structural Disruptions, Policy Lock-in, and the Case for a 2050 Existential Resilience Framework
affiliations: Libyan Authority for Scientific Research

detail.title:
Beyond the 2030 Agenda: 
Structural Disruptions, Policy Lock-in, and the Case for a 2050 Existential Resilience Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study as it relies exclusively on publicly available secondary data and theoretical analysis, involving no human participants, animal subjects, or sensitive personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. This study was entirely self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
By 2025, only 18% of SDG indicators are on track, 48% show insufficient progress, and 18% have regressed below 2015 baselines (UN DESA, 2025). The dominant explanation-financing gaps and weak implementation-misidentifies the problem. This article argues that three compounding structural disruptions have rendered the 2030 Agenda's foundational assumptions obsolete: a sovereign debt crisis that now transfers $405 billion annually from developing nations to Global North creditors; the return of active armed great-power rivalry and the weaponization of global economic interdependence; and the displacement of routine cognitive labor by advanced AI automation systems that are eliminating the comparative advantage on which Global South development strategies have depended. Together, these disruptions have dissolved the conditions of peace, open trade, and human-centric productivity that the Agenda requires. No financing increase restores them. We propose the 2050 Existential Resilience Framework (ERF), organized around three operational pillars-technological sovereignty, closed-loop resource autonomy, and asymmetric human capital-and operationalized through a Democratic Governance Interface comprising Polycentric Deliberative Assemblies, a Global Technology and Resource Commons, and equityweighted adaptation metrics anchored to the lowest-income decile. 

      The analytical approach is Critical Narrative Analysis supported by secondary indicators and scenario foresight, drawing on verified multilateral datasets, peer-reviewed labor and development economics, and structured scenario methodology. The ERF is not a preferred vision; it is a defensive response to documented structural failure. It's most serious risk-that resilience logic reproduces and deepens existing inequalities-is examined with the seriousness it deserves.

title: Classical and Quantum Equilibria in Bayesian Games ⋆
affiliations: University of Rochester

detail.title: Classical and Quantum Equilibria in Bayesian Games ⋆
detail.abstract: Players in a Bayesian game are forbidden to share their private signals with anyone, including a referee; each player can condition her action only on phenomena she observes directly. We classify Bayes correlated equilibria by the resources required to implement them privately. Some arise from strategic-form correlated equilibria and can be implemented by a signal-blind referee. A strictly larger class can be implemented with classical correlating devices: we exhibit an equilibrium implementable by such devices but by no referee, strengthening a known separation between strategic-form and agent-normal-form correlated equilibrium. A larger class still becomes implementable with quantum devices, and quantum-implementable equilibria can be Pareto-superior to every classical equilibrium-even in games where the players' interests conflict. The paper presupposes no familiarity with quantum mechanics and is intended to double as an introduction to quantum game theory for economists.

title: The Acceleration Balance Equation (ABE): A Unified Physics-Based Framework for Modeling and Forecasting Complex Time Series
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Acceleration Balance Equation (ABE): A Unified Physics-Based Framework for Modeling and Forecasting Complex Time Series
detail.abstract:
This four-paper series presents the theoretical, mathematical, computational, and interpretative foundations of the Acceleration Balance Equation (ABE) framework, a physics-based approach for the analysis and forecasting of complex time series. ABE is developed from physical analogies with fluid dynamics and dynamical systems, translating the evolution of a time series into interpretable quantities such as density, velocity, pressure, viscosity, acceleration, and interaction forces. The complete framework is organized as a progressive research ecosystem comprising 1ABE, nABE, LABE, and GABE, together with a fourth complementary article devoted to additional mathematical developments, uncertainty measures, dependencies, and theoretical extensions.

The first article introduces 1ABE, the one-dimensional formulation of the Acceleration Balance Equation. A single time series is represented as a dynamical system whose temporal evolution results from the balance between internal and external acceleration components. The formulation establishes the fundamental physical variables of ABE and develops a practical forecasting methodology. In preliminary financial applications, 1ABE has shown particularly promising performance in directional forecasting, with accuracy reaching approximately 85% for certain analyzed assets, while also revealing that different time series exhibit different levels of predictability and dynamical structure.

The second article extends this formulation to nABE, a multidimensional framework for systems composed of multiple interacting time series. nABE is formulated as a weighted extension of Navier–Stokes-inspired dynamics to n dimensions, incorporating the influence of other series through interaction structures and relative importance coefficients. This formulation provides a natural generalization of 1ABE and is intended to improve the description of systems in which the evolution of an individual variable cannot be understood independently of the variables surrounding it.

The third article introduces the variational and geometric extensions LABE (Lagrangian Acceleration Balance Equation) and GABE (Geodesic Acceleration Balance Equation). LABE reformulates ABE through the Principle of Least Action, defining a Lagrangian and an associated action for possible future trajectories. This makes it possible to move from a single deterministic forecast toward a probabilistic description of alternative future states, in which dynamically preferred trajectories are associated with lower action. GABE further develops this interpretation geometrically, describing the evolution of the system through preferred paths or geodesics within the dynamical structure generated by ABE.

The fourth article complements the three principal formulations by collecting and developing mathematical, physical, statistical, and interpretative aspects that are not essential to the presentation of the individual models but are important for understanding the complete ABE framework. These include additional derivations, relationships between physical quantities, measures of information and dependence between time series, uncertainty coefficients, theoretical interpretations, and further connections with mathematical physics and complex-system analysis.

Taken together, the four articles propose ABE as a unified framework in which dynamics, interaction, variational principles, probability, geometry, and uncertainty can be studied within a common mathematical structure. Rather than treating a time series exclusively as a statistical sequence of observations, ABE interprets it as the observable evolution of a dynamical system governed by measurable balances and interactions. The resulting framework is intended both as a forecasting methodology and as a broader research program for investigating financial, economic, and other complex temporal systems.

title: Eco-capitalism or Greenwashing? Analyzing the Political Economy of Carbon Markets and their Impact on Global Inequality

detail.title: Eco-capitalism or Greenwashing? Analyzing the Political Economy of Carbon Markets and their Impact on Global Inequality
detail.abstract: With CO₂ concentrations exceeding 420 parts per million and unmitigated climate change costs estimated at five to twenty percent of global GDP, carbon markets have become central to international climate governance. This paper asks whether these mechanisms deliver genuine emissions reductions or function as structural greenwashing, enabling wealthy states and corporations to avoid systemic change. Drawing on political economy and environmental justice theory, the study applies comparative case analysis to the EU Emissions Trading System, California's cap-and-trade programme, and carbon offset dynamics in sub-Saharan Africa. The EU ETS cut covered-sector emissions by 37 percent between 2005 and 2022 under stringent conditions, yet such governance remains structurally exceptional. Where caps are weak and offset integrity limited, markets deepen inequalities, reproduce colonial extraction patterns, and generate gender-inequitable outcomes. Examining environmental effectiveness and distributive justice in conjunction, the paper advances a political economy framework foregrounding power asymmetries and structural inequality, concluding with recommendations for justice-centred reform integrating market mechanisms with direct regulation and redistributive fiscal policy.

title: Trade Secret Protection in the Indian Software Industry: Examining Legal Gaps and Their Implications on Innovation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and St.Joseph’s Institute of Technology

detail.title: Trade Secret Protection in the Indian Software Industry: Examining Legal Gaps and Their Implications on Innovation
detail.abstract: In India's software industry, increasingly depends on valuable intellectual assets such as proprietary source code, algorithms, technical know-how and other confidential information. While existing intellectual property laws provide different forms of protection under section 3(k) of the Indian patent Act, 1970 that aligned with Trips Article 27, computer program per se and algorithms are excluded from patent protection. Although patent Act provides patent for certain software programs it does not define, within the statutory provision itself resulting in reliance of guidelines and judicial precedents. Furthermore, while the copyright Act, 1957 protects original source code, it covers only literal expression, leaving underlying functional logic and algorithms vulnerable to reverse engineering. These limitations make the protection of confidential software information particularly significant. Although Article 39 of the Trips Agreement mandates robust protection for undisclosed information, India lacks a dedicated sui generis trade secret statute, relying instead on contract law, common law breach of trust and the Information Technology Act, 2000. This research employs a Doctrinal research methodology, this study analyses primary domestic statutes, international treaties, judicial precedents and the 22 nd Law Commission's 289 th report. This paper demonstrates the urgent need for a codified trade secret law in India to resolve existing legal uncertainties and fulfil India's commitments under Trips Article 39.

title: Tight Capital, Loose Money: How Stress-Tested Banks Responded to Quantitative Easing
affiliations: London Business School, Department of Finance, London Business School and London Business School

detail.title: Tight Capital, Loose Money: How Stress-Tested Banks Responded to Quantitative Easing
detail.abstract: We study how bank capital regulation shapes the transmission of quantitative easing (QE) to borrowers. Exploiting differences in exposure to post-crisis stress tests across U.S. banks during the Federal Reserve's asset purchases, and using granular loan-rate data, we find that stress-tested banks reduced mortgage rates more but increased consumer loan rates more. These effects are strongest for banks required to raise the most capital and those most exposed to the Fed's mortgage-backed security purchases. An estimated model shows that capital-constrained banks reallocate lending toward mortgages, whose funding costs QE lowers, and away from consumer credit. Capital regulation thus redirects monetary stimulus across credit markets.

detail.abstract: Traditional banking systems rely on severely lagged indicators-such as 30-, 60-, or 90-day delinquency reports-to monitor mortgage credit risk. However, financially distressed homeowners exhibit behavioral shifts in digital search behavior months before missing their first mortgage payment. This paper develops an empirical framework that constructs a realtime, high-frequency Platform Search Distress Index (𝑆 𝑗𝑡) by tracking normalized search ratios between low-cost rental platforms (e.g., Craigslist, Apartments.com) and home-buying platforms (e.g., Zillow). Using a Cox proportional hazard model combined with a panel fixedeffects predictive regression across U.S. zip codes, we demonstrate that a sustained spike in 𝑆 𝑗𝑡 leads official bank default servicing logs by 3 to 6 months. Furthermore, embedding digital search metrics alongside conventional Combined Loan-to-Value (CLTV) and Debt-to-Income (DTI) ratios significantly improves out-of-sample forecast accuracy for localized default waves. The framework provides central banks, bank supervisors, and mortgage-backed securities (MBS) investors with a real-time macroprudential risk dashboard.
