detail.abstract: Traditional contingent-claims models of mortgage valuation treat household inertia, search frictions, and transaction costs as static parameters. However, the rapid proliferation of property technology (PropTech) platforms and continuous Automated Valuation Models (AVMs) has fundamentally restructured the information topology of residential housing markets. This paper develops a dynamic, continuous-time structural model of mortgage default and prepayment that explicitly incorporates platform-driven valuation transparency (𝜃 AVM) and rental market search efficiency (𝜃 search). We prove that digital aggregators systematically compress the household inaction region (hysteresis band) by reducing price monitoring costs and relocation transaction frictions. Consequently, threshold boundaries for both prepayment and strategic default sharpen, increasing the velocity and elasticity of default responses to negative equity shocks. Expanding the framework, we outline macroprudential implications for mortgage-backed securities (MBS) pricing and propose an empirical research agenda for testing platform-mediated credit contagion.

title: Selling a Single Item: A Mean-Variance Approach
affiliations: Google Inc. - Google Zürich and National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

detail.title: Selling a Single Item: A Mean-Variance Approach
detail.abstract: We study the optimal selling of a single item when the seller is risk-averse and evaluates revenue using a mean-variance objective. We consider two canonical transfer timing models. In Model A (interim transfer timing), the interim payment associated with the buyer's type is paid deterministically, so the seller's risk comes only from type uncertainty. Under a natural risk regularity condition, we characterize the optimal incentive-compatible mechanism via an optimal control approach, showing that it consists of a full allocation region, an interior screening region governed by a first-order ODE with a closed-form solution, and an exclusion region. The resulting allocation is continuous, and this continuity conclusion holds even without risk regularity. In Model B (ex post transfer timing), payment occurs only upon allocation, exposing the seller to additional allocation-lottery risk. Our main result is that, under Myerson regularity, this extra risk overturns the continuous-screening logic familiar from interimtransfer models: a posted price is globally optimal among all incentive-compatible and interim-IR mechanisms. The optimal posted price also satisfies ex post IR, so strengthening the participation requirement does not change the seller's optimal value. The contrast is sharp: the canonical right-continuous representative of every optimal Model A allocation is continuous on (0, 1), whereas Model B admits an optimal cutoff rule that is discontinuous whenever the optimal trade probability is interior. We also discuss why extending the posted-price characterization beyond Myerson-regular distributions requires new arguments.

title: Informal Networks and Knowledge Flows
affiliations: Tuck School of Business and Babson College

detail.title: Informal Networks and Knowledge Flows
detail.abstract: Informal networks serve as the 'central nervous systems' of organizations, shaping how knowledge flows between individuals and gets transformed into value for the firm. While formal organizational structures establish official channels of communication, individuals often bypass them in favor of emergent, informal relationships to access information from across the organization. This chapter examines the structural, social, and cognitive mechanisms that shape knowledge flows through informal networks, with particular attention to the characteristics of the individual, the dyad, the organization, and the knowledge itself. We situate this informal network perspective within broader organizational design considerations, drawing connections to the roles of physical space, proximity, and the interplay between formal and informal structures. In addition to reviewing contemporary research on knowledge flows, we identify promising areas for future research, including the ways in which technology and distributed work arrangements are reshaping how knowledge is accessed and shared, and the methodological advances and new data sources that are expanding scholars' ability to study these open questions with greater precision and causal rigor. We conclude by contending that informal networks should be thought of as a core strategic asset and, while they cannot be entirely designed, organizations can play an active role in shaping the opportunities and conditions for knowledge transfer. As such, informal network should be central in conversations around organizational design and the pursuit of organizational goals.

title: On the Evolution of the General Equilibrium Model: A Regime-Contingent Extension for Trade Barriers Under Geoeconomic Fragmentation
affiliations: Southern Federal University

detail.title: On the Evolution of the General Equilibrium Model: A Regime-Contingent Extension for Trade Barriers Under Geoeconomic Fragmentation
detail.abstract: The article traces the evolution of the general equilibrium model, from the classical concept developed by Léon Walras to modern computable and dynamic stochastic models, showing that successive generations of the theory have advanced chiefly by endogenizing assumptions that earlier models treated as fixed. Building on this historical account, the article proposes an original extension of the classical two-country partial equilibrium trade framework in which the bilateral trade cost is treated not as a fixed parameter but as a function of a discrete geopolitical-regime variable. A formal trade-diversion result is derived, showing that a deterioration in the political relationship between trading partners generates a discontinuous reallocation of trade volumes toward geopolitically closer destinations, even absent any change in the underlying technology or preferences of the parties involved. The proposed extension is shown to rationalize patterns of commodity-export reorientation documented in the recent geoeconomic-fragmentation literature, situating them within the broader historical trajectory of general equilibrium theory.

title: 2026 National Firearms Survey: Results from the Second Wave, Including Current Ownership of AR-15 Style Rifles, Other "Assault Weapons," and Magazines that Hold More than 10 Rounds
affiliations: McDonough School of Business, Georgetown University

detail.title: 2026 National Firearms Survey: Results from the Second Wave, Including Current Ownership of AR-15 Style Rifles, Other "Assault Weapons," and Magazines that Hold More than 10 Rounds

declarations.ethicsApproval: This survey was IRB approved.
declarations.funderStatement: This survey and research was supported by a grant from the Wealth of Nations Institute.

detail.abstract:
This report summarizes the findings of the second wave of the National Firearms Survey, a national survey of firearms ownership and use conducted in July and August of 2026. The survey was administered online to a representative sample of 51,398 U.S. residents aged 18 and over, and it identified 16,688 internally validated gun owners who answered in-depth questions concerning their ownership and use of firearms, including questions about using a firearm in self-defense. The second wave incorporates a series of methodological refinements that respond directly to scholarly discussion of the first (2021) wave: ownership questions specify individual rather than household or spousal ownership; questions about magazines and “assault weapons” ask about current rather than past ownership; AR-15 type rifles and other similarly styled semi-automatic rifles are asked about separately; respondents who report defensive gun uses are asked the approximate age at which each incident occurred and whether the defensive use succeeded in averting a crime (or was directed against an animal threat); and, as a two-stage data-integrity check, respondents are counted as gun owners only if they both indicated firearm ownership on a screening question and subsequently reported owning a positive number of rifles, shotguns, or handguns in a detailed count of firearm types that required a response. In addition, the analyzed sample reflects standard quality-control checks, including an embedded attention check and the removal of responses with low reCAPTCHA scores and suspected duplicate responses.

With raked weighting on gender, age, race, and state of residence, using targets from the 2024 American Community Survey, the survey finds that 32.7% of U.S. adults (95% CI 32.2% – 33.2%) personally own firearms, suggesting that approximately 88 million American adults own guns. Following the practice of major survey programs such as the General Social Survey, Gallup, and Pew’s American Trends Panel, household income is not employed as a weighting dimension. However, income-raked estimates, which range up to 34.9%, are reported as robustness exercises in an appendix. Ownership is demographically diverse: 45.7% of validated gun owners are female, 25.6% do not identify as White (alone), and the gap in ownership rates between White Americans (34.6%) and Black Americans (33.0%) has narrowed to less than two percentage points. The survey finds that 37.6% of gun owners have used a firearm to defend themselves, their property, a family member, or a member of their household, and it estimates that guns are used defensively by firearms owners in approximately 2.2 million incidents per year. In most defensive incidents no shot was fired (76.3%), about half (50.8%) involved more than one assailant, and in 70.6% of incidents respondents report that the defensive use was successful, such that no crime remained to be reported to the police. 8.4% of defensive incidents were directed against animal threats rather than criminal threats. Separate from these self-defense incidents, 34.7% of gun owners reported that the mere presence of a gun has deterred criminal conduct.

A majority of gun owners (70.0%) indicate that there are some circumstances in which they carry a handgun for self-defense. We estimate that approximately 33.6 million gun owners (39.3% of those aged 21 and over) are “public carriers” who are permitted to carry and carry at least sometimes. The average gun owner owns about 5.2 firearms, and handguns are the most common type of firearm owned (91.6% of owners). 50.5% of gun owners – approximately 44.5 million adults – report that they currently own magazines that hold more than 10 rounds (approximately 539 million such magazines in total), and 88.0% of these owners cite a defensive purpose for owning them. 25.0% of gun owners currently own an AR-15 type rifle, 12.9% currently own other similarly styled semi-automatic rifles, and 30.0% – approximately 26.4 million adults – currently own at least one firearm in one of these two categories, with approximately 40 million AR-15 type rifles and 20 million other similarly styled rifles owned in total. Overall, Americans own approximately 461 million firearms, consisting of approximately 208 million handguns, 154 million rifles, and 99 million shotguns.

detail.abstract: The article critically examines the simplification rationale underlying the Omnibus amendments to the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D), contending that simplification need not entail a reduction in the scope or effectiveness of corporate due diligence obligations. It identifies key shortcomings in the current approach, including limiting due diligence duties to direct business partners, weakening of stakeholder involvement, and undermining the complementarity between administrative and judicial enforcement.

title: Democratizing Private Markets: Equilibrium Predictions
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Democratizing Private Markets: Equilibrium Predictions
detail.abstract: We study how opening private markets to retail investors affects investors and firms.  Calibrating a production-based asset-pricing model, we find that democratization raises retail investors' welfare, but barely.  Retail investors benefit little from democratization even if they face no extra cost or other disadvantage relative to institutional investors. The private market is simply too small for improved risk sharing to matter much.  Whether or not private-market retail investing is costly, democratization substantially reshapes private firms' ownership and materially reduces their cost of capital, leading them to grow.  Private equity earns a positive CAPM alpha, which shrinks after democratization.

title: The Public Utility Tradition in Antitrust Remedies
affiliations: Vanderbilt Law School

detail.title: The Public Utility Tradition in Antitrust Remedies
detail.abstract:
Historically, courts, jurists, legislatures, and scholars have recognized that some businesses provide important services to society in sectors in which competition is unlikely to achieve the public interest. Policymakers adopted statutes that comprehensively regulated the market structure and operations of these businesses as public utilities, including, among other things, by determining entry and exit into business lines; overseeing or affirmatively setting prices; and requiring uniform, nondiscriminatory sales and access. When policymakers had not—or had not yet––stepped in to legislatively regulate these enterprises, abuses of power were possible. Private plaintiffs and governments sued under the common law or antitrust laws to redress anticompetitive, unfair, or otherwise abusive practices. Importantly, when they won, courts regularly applied what we would today call the tools of networks, platforms, and utilities (“NPU”) law to the enterprise as a remedy. Cases in this tradition include some of the most famous in antitrust law and in their respective sectors. In other words, regulatory absences gave rise to antitrust remedies. 

The public utility tradition in antitrust remedies sheds light on a range of debates and puzzles. First, it helps clarify and contributes to understanding the relationship between antitrust and regulation, suggesting that rather than being substitutes, antitrust operates more like a backstop. Second, it suggests that NPU regulation may be inevitable in many sectors. The question is whether NPU tools should be adopted legislatively or via remedies, not whether they should apply. Third, the public utility tradition helps make sense of the essential facilities doctrine in antitrust law, which requires the owner of an enterprise that is essential and not readily replicable to serve users on fair terms. A sensible way to interpret the doctrine is that it applies to unregulated public utilities. Finally, the public utility tradition in antitrust remedies supports the case for bolder remedies—and makes sense of the proposed remedies—in the antitrust cases against technology platforms.

title: The House Doesn't Know Your Credit Score: Place as a Second Dimension of Mortgage Risk
affiliations: Ross School of Business, University of Michigan

detail.title: The House Doesn't Know Your Credit Score: Place as a Second Dimension of Mortgage Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: See text

detail.abstract: Two borrowers can carry the same credit score and still face wildly different odds of default, for a reason that has nothing to do with either of them: where they live. This paper argues that place—the shifting economic, demographic, and housing conditions of a local market—is a second dimension of mortgage risk, as consequential as the borrower's credit history and largely independent of it. Mortgage models have long treated collateral value as something to check once, at the appraisal, and then forget. But a house is not a fact; it is a claim on the future of a neighborhood, and that future is written by local employment, migration, and construction, not by the borrower. Using 47,000 mortgage originations tracked for seven years, I sort loans by credit score and by a composite measure of local market strength (ForeScore™). Borrowers with a credit score near 631 default at 4 percent in the strongest markets and 19 percent in the weakest—nearly a fivefold gap among people who, on paper, look the same. Credit score keeps sorting risk inside every market tier; place keeps sorting risk inside every credit tier. Neither swallows the other. I connect this finding to the existing default literature—strong on negative equity and liquidity shocks, thinner on systematic measurement of the local environment—and draw out what it means for underwriting, loss severity, and stress testing.

title: Designing AI-Augmented Peer Review

detail.title: Designing AI-Augmented Peer Review

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rotman School of Management Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: AI-generated assessments of manuscripts could improve the quality of peer review, but sharing them with reviewers might decrease the information that editors possess about the manuscript. Human peer reviews add value because reviewers add what the AI assessment reveals. When both reviewers see the same assessment and make similar errors, they can replicate each other's mistakes, coincidentally investigate related areas, and share the same blind spots. If AI assessment improves the quality of reviewers' work while they investigate the manuscript, giving the report to only one reviewer can better combine AI assistance with independent, human investigation. If some reviewers already use AI-generated assessments on their own, changing the journal policy to allow sharing the assessment can improve peer review if the change takes some of the burden of investigation off private tools that make similar errors, though giving the assessment to only one reviewer may still outperform giving it to both or neither. Even a report delivered after the reviews are submitted can still shift what reviewers investigate if they know in advance which issues it will check. Journal policy will depend on the AI's effects on reviewer effort and the questions they investigate, whether reviewers are willing and able to comply with the policy, the monitoring costs, and the journal's ability to protect the confidentiality of reviewer identities and emails. Journals can evaluate competing policies without knowing the true quality of the manuscripts they review by randomly varying who receives the assessment and then comparing reviewer disagreement across different levels of report sharing.

detail.title: Microfinance Borrowers' Challenges in Odisha: Evidence from a Primary Survey

publicationDetails.detailsText: The IUP Journal of Bank Management, 25(3), 58-83

detail.abstract: This study examines the issues and challenges faced by microfinance institution (MFI) borrowers in Odisha using primary survey data across five districts based on borrower and credit concentration. The findings reveal that while MFIs significantly enhance financial inclusion and livelihood opportunities, borrowers reported that they face relatively higher interest rates, loan processing fees, and, in a few cases, rigid weekly repayment schedules. The survey also highlights gaps in borrower awareness and institutional practices. The random forest analysis, an ensemble learning method that constructs a multitude of decision trees and aggregates their predictions, reveals that borrowers with higher loan amounts express concerns over higher processing and insurance fees.

title: Production Network Position and Inventory Management Efficiency
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China and Durham University Business School, Finance and Economics

detail.title: Production Network Position and Inventory Management Efficiency
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether a firm’s sectoral position in the production network affects its inventory management efficiency. Using China’s input–output tables, we construct an inter-sector network and measure sector centrality using closeness centrality. We find that firms operating in more central sectors exhibit significantly higher inventory turnover, with a stronger effect among non-state-owned and more diversified firms, as well as under higher demand uncertainty, greater supply chain disruption risks, and more intense market competition. Our findings identify production network centrality as an important determinant of inventory efficiency and highlight the role of information embedded in production networks in shaping firms’ operational outcomes.

title: Conference Governance
affiliations: University of Iowa

detail.title: Conference Governance
detail.abstract:
The recent and significant changes in college athletics have led to both perceived chaos within the industry and increased scrutiny of the NCAA and its ability to effectively govern. While many consider alternate governance models, some prominent athletics conferences commissioners have publicly hinted at the likelihood of increased conference involvement in college athletics governance, which put the national media in a frenzy. 

This article examines conferences' current involvement in college athletics governance, concluding not only that conferences' current role in governance is underappreciated but an increase in their involvement could lead to significant benefits including mitigated antitrust exposure. In doing so, the article examines the current governance model in Division I and explores some examples of conference-level governance that have already taken place. The article then analyzes two recent federal court decisions that concluded that individual conferences' lack of market power provides them with rule making and enforcement flexibility that the NCAA may no longer enjoy under antitrust law.

title: BlightLens: Detecting and Prioritizing Tulsa Housing Blight with AI
affiliations: University of Tulsa, The University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, University of Tulsa, , University of Tulsa - Collins College of Business and University of Tulsa

detail.title: BlightLens: Detecting and Prioritizing Tulsa Housing Blight with AI
detail.abstract: This project is focused on increasing our understanding of the causes blighted (vacant, abandoned, or dilapidated) housing. Previous research on blighted housing has largely focused on quantifying the negative effects of blight to property values, neighborhoods, and other socioeconomic outcomes of interest. There is a limited body of empirical work, largely case studies, describing city-specific efforts and incentives to reduce blighted housing. The aim of this project is to develop a broadly generalizable methodology to 1) Rapidly and objectively identify blighted housing at the property level using AI workflows that incorporates quantitative, textual, and visual data points and 2) Develop an understanding of early warning signs for severe housing blight to recommend strategies for policymakers to perform cost-effective early intervention to reduce blight. Our work focuses on single family detached houses located within the boundaries of the City of Tulsa. However, the aim of the research is not to simply perform a large-scale case study, but to develop insights and employable methodologies that are broadly relevant to other mid-sized US cities with significant underutilized housing stock.

title: Joint estimation of multiple cardiovascular parameters from blood pressure waveforms using multi-task learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Seoul National University - Seoul National University Hospital, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Joint estimation of multiple cardiovascular parameters from blood pressure waveforms using multi-task learning
detail.abstract: Background and Objective:Estimation of cardiovascular parameters is essential for the assessment of cardiovascular health. Blood pressure waveforms are usually used for an efficient and continuous cardiovascular evaluation in practical clinical settings. However, previous studies have focused mainly on the independent estimation of vascular age, stroke volume, or peripheral resistance, while joint estimation within a unified framework remains underexplored. Methods:Since cardiovascular parameters jointly influence blood pressure waveform morphology, tasks for estimating cardiovascular parameters can be regarded as related tasks. Therefore, we formulated joint cardiovascular parameter estimation as a multi-task learning problem. However, since cardiovascular parameters effect different temporal regions in the blood pressure waveform, naive multi-task learning architecture can suffer negative transfer. So, we proposed a cross-talk architecture, residual neural dimension reductor with temporal and channel attention (RNDR-TCA), which models nonlinear inter-task relations while preserving task-specific representations through residual connections. Additionally, temporal and channel attention modules enhance intra-task temporal features and inter-task features, respectively. Experimental validation was conducted using a physiologically credible cardiovascular simulator dataset, where the values of independently controlled cardiovascular parameters were treated as classes for estimation based on value classification.Results:RNDR-TCA achieved the highest average Macro F1 score of 0.836, outperforming separate single-task learning models (0.784), multi-class classifier (0.771), shared-trunk architectures (0.781-0.816), and existing cross-talk architectures (0.792-0.824).Conclusions:The proposed RNDR-TCA effectively leverages inter-task relations for joint cardiovascular parameter estimation from blood pressure waveforms. The results suggest that attention-enhanced cross-talk architectures can improve multi-parameter cardiovascular assessment using a unified deep learning framework.

title: The Crypto Cycle and Institutional Investors
affiliations: International Monetary Fund, affiliation not provided to SSRN and IESE Business School

detail.title: The Crypto Cycle and Institutional Investors
detail.abstract: We examine aggregate fluctuations in crypto markets and their relationship to global equity markets and US monetary policy. First, we document that changes in the correlation between crypto and global equity markets can be explained by changes in the participation of institutional investors in crypto markets. Second, we find that US monetary policy significantly affects crypto markets, but only when the participation of institutional investors is high. Third, within high-participation periods, the response is concentrated where the leverage of crypto investors, measured by the perpetual-futures funding rate, is high. Finally, we rationalize our empirical results in a heterogeneous-agent model in which large investors holding both asset classes create a direct link between them, and the effective risk aversion of the crypto market is governed by their balance-sheet constraints.

title: Intensified Plasmid Capture Process via Continuous Lysis and Membrane Chromatography
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Intensified Plasmid Capture Process via Continuous Lysis and Membrane Chromatography
detail.abstract: The growing demand for plasmid DNA (pDNA) driven by advancements in gene therapy and vaccines calls for efficient and scalable production methods. Traditional batch E. coli lysis methods are constrained by the mixing process, as it lacks consistent control of lysis time, and involves local high shear forces and extreme pH, potentially compromising the plasmid quality during scale-up. Further, purification steps with resin-based columns are time-consuming and require additional operations, such as RNA precipitation and tangential flow filtration. This work presents an intensified pDNA production process based on a continuous cell lysis device that integrates low-shear pumps and a loop reactor to precisely control lysis time while minimizing shear damage. Coupled with membrane chromatography, this process enables high flow rates and effective RNA reduction without requiring RNase or other chemicals, simply by optimizing the load material's conductivity. This results in a faster and more cost-effective pDNA production process with high yields and purity, which was demonstrated for different plasmid constructs of various sizes.

title: From Payer to Provider: Impacts of Insurer Vertical Expansion into Physician Services
affiliations: Brown University, Brown University and Brown University

detail.title: From Payer to Provider: Impacts of Insurer Vertical Expansion into Physician Services
detail.abstract: Vertical integration can both create efficiencies and harm competition through rival foreclosure. We examine these tensions through one of the most prominent forms of vertical integration in the United States: the acquisition of physician practices by the nation’s largest insurer, UnitedHealth Group. Using a difference-in-differences design and Medicare administrative data, we find minimal changes to acquired practice case mix or care quality, but do find evidence of increased patient risk score coding intensity, which translate into nearly \$300 million in annual increased spending. However, due the absence of rival foreclosure, the majority of this transfer payment accrues to rival firms.

title: The Erasure Reflex: Identity Threat, Institutional Unconscious, and Defensive Erasure Across Social Levels
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Erasure Reflex: Identity Threat, Institutional Unconscious, and Defensive Erasure Across Social Levels
detail.abstract:
This study develops the concept of the Erasure Reflex to explain how individuals and organizations may respond to identity- or legitimacy-threatening information by reducing connections with the person associated with that information rather than directly resolving its substantive content. Erasure does not necessarily involve physical removal or formal exclusion. Instead, it may emerge gradually as conversational, informational, relational, and occupational connections are repeatedly reduced, leaving a person formally included while progressively diminishing their substantive participation.

Building on Silent Harassment, Institutional Unconscious, Structural Monster, and the Fractal Defense Model, the study integrates research on identity threat, organizational silence, workplace ostracism, threat rigidity, legitimacy, employee voice, and whistleblowing. At the individual level, threatening information may become associated with a particular person, making contact with that person a recurrent source of threat exposure. When avoidance produces short-term relief, repeated connection reduction may develop into Relational Erasure. At the organizational level, problem raising that challenges legitimacy or established order may be translated through the Institutional Unconscious into administratively manageable issues involving procedure, responsibility, roles, and access, potentially producing Occupational Erasure. These 1 processes do not share an identical psychological mechanism; rather, they become functionally self-similar because both reduce substantive connections with a threat-associated target.

The study further introduces Control-Target Substitution (CTS), whereby defensive control shifts from threatening information to its relatively more controllable carrier as the information itself becomes increasingly difficult to contain, alter, or retract. It also proposes the Erasure Paradox, whereby declining internal visibility may coexist with increasing external informational persistence when experiences are recorded, preserved, and externalized by the target or by third parties. Erasure may therefore become self-defeating under conditions of sustained documentation and externalization. Furthermore, when the target continues to observe subsequent defensive responses and transforms them into new objects of documentation, conceptualization, and externalization, Recursive Externalization may enable external information to accumulate over time.

The Erasure Reflex reframes erasure not simply as an intentional act of exclusion but as a possible emergent outcome of repeated local attempts to reduce exposure to threatening information. By distinguishing Person Avoidance from Problem Resolution, the framework explains how defensive actions that provide short-term stability may, under certain conditions, inhibit organizational learning and generate unintended long-term consequences.

title: Machiavelli: From the Battlefield to the Boardroom

detail.title: Machiavelli: From the Battlefield to the Boardroom

detail.abstract: Strategic power is often described through possession: armies, territory, capital, technology, industrial capacity, market share, infrastructure, or political authority. Yet possession matters strategically only when it alters what another actor can do, believes it can do, wants to do, or can afford to do. This essay develops a grammar of strategic power organized around four recurring forms of pressure: coercion, which raises the cost of refusal; dependency, which narrows feasible alternatives; competitive provision, which improves an alternative; and expressive power, which changes how alternatives are understood, valued, or legitimized. These forms are analytical dimensions rather than deterministic causes or mutually exclusive categories. Their effects are mediated by interpretation, time, autonomy, institutional structure, history, identity, and human judgment. The framework therefore treats strategy as recursive: strategic pressure is interpreted, produces a response, changes the surrounding structure, and generates new pressures. It further argues that strategic intelligence is institutionally produced through framing, collection, selection, interpretation, dissemination, reception, and judgment; no single intelligence tradition possesses universal epistemic authority. The appropriate ambition is consequently anticipation rather than prediction: identifying consequential possibilities, recognizing movement among them, and preserving sufficient freedom to adapt. Machiavellian virtù is recast as an institutional capacity to frame problems from competing perspectives, preserve dissent, integrate plural forms of knowledge, commit under uncertainty, and revise before failure makes revision unavoidable. Strategy can be disciplined without becoming mechanical.

title: The Innovation Capacity Loop: Technology, Capacity, and the Rise of Machine Innovation

detail.title: The Innovation Capacity Loop: Technology, Capacity, and the Rise of Machine Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Innovation Capacity Loop (ICL), a theory explaining how technology can create a self-reinforcing cycle in which technological progress increases the capacity available to produce the next generation of innovation. The basic loop is: technology increases productivity → creates potential surplus → some surplus is realized and directed toward innovation → innovation capacity increases → new technology is produced → the cycle begins again. Historically, the loop depended primarily on humans to turn technological gains into further innovation, but AI and advanced robotics may fundamentally change its structure by increasingly participating directly in innovation-producing work. The result could be a coupled human–machine Innovation Capacity Loop, in which humans improve machines, machines increase human innovative capacity and contribute directly to innovation, and each round of technological progress expands the capacity available for the next round—making technological advancement increasingly self-reinforcing and less dependent on proportional increases in human innovative effort.

title: News Consumption in the Digital Age
affiliations: University of Barcelona - Institut d'Economia de Barcelona (IEB), , University of Cologne and University of Cologne

detail.title: News Consumption in the Digital Age
detail.abstract: Digital technologies have transformed the news landscape, shifting consumption from print media toward online providers. This has allowed news outlets to collect richer data on individual readers, and to use those data both to tailor the news a reader sees — which stories appear and how they are framed — and to sell more precisely targeted advertising. Online news outlets also increasingly recruit readers from social media, amplifying incentives to capture reader attention through sensationalized stories and other techniques to increase engagement. Generative AI is likely to accelerate this trend by lowering the cost of personalizing news. Whether cheaper production and finer personalization raise or lower consumer welfare depends on how closely the objectives firms maximize are aligned with the underlying preferences of consumers. This review studies how the shift toward online news consumption affects both the supply and the demand for news and draws potential implications for consumer welfare.

title: Hidden Capacity Theory: How Crossing Perceived Limits Changes Future Effort

detail.title: Hidden Capacity Theory: How Crossing Perceived Limits Changes Future Effort
detail.abstract: People often stop at boundaries that feel real even when additional capacity remains available. Hidden Capacity Theory (HCT) explains how crossing one of those boundaries can change future effort long after the unusual motivation that produced the crossing has disappeared. People learn where to stop from experience, using fatigue, discomfort, cognitive strain, declining performance, and other cues to judge when further effective effort is no longer available. Those judgments are useful, but they are not perfect observations of maximum capacity. When consequential circumstances lead a person to continue beyond a familiar stopping point and effective performance continues, the episode provides evidence that the old boundary was too low or that the cue used to locate it was less reliable than previously believed. If the person treats that evidence as informative about personal capacity, a limit reset can occur. The person need not discover a true maximum. It is enough to learn that a cue that once meant “I cannot continue effectively” is no longer sufficient evidence to stop. HCT explains when effort becomes information about capacity and why that information can continue to shape behavior after the circumstances that produced it are gone. The theory distinguishes this mechanism from generalized mastery-based efficacy updating, motivational intensity, learned industriousness, reserve-capacity approaches, and stretch-goal theory, while also showing how visible demonstrations of capacity can create organizational expectations before the costs of sustaining that performance become clear.

detail.abstract: This study examines how institutional climate communication campaigns associated with 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28) strategically deploy multimedia and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted tools across social media platforms to shape public engagement. Adopting a mixed-methods research design, the study combines quantitative analysis of platform engagement metrics using PLS-SEM modeling with a complementary qualitative thematic reading of publicly available audience comments on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, X (Twitter), and LinkedIn. The quantitative findings indicate that semantic-rich video content is positively associated with higher audience engagement (β = 0.50, p = 0.007), AIenabled content personalization is associated with improved campaign effectiveness measured through click-through and conversion indicators (β = 0.42, p = 0.020), and interactive multimedia features are associated with stronger user interaction and retention (β = 0.57, p = 0.004). These results are interpreted through media richness and social presence perspectives, alongside platform-based communication logics that emphasize the role of algorithmic visibility, datadriven optimization, and sociotechnical affordances in shaping institutional publics online. The study contributes to social media scholarship by extending empirical evidence on AI-mediated multimedia engagement to the domain of institutional climate communication, while highlighting implications for responsible personalization, transparency, and public trust within platform environments.

title: The Human-Machine Knowledge Gap: When Knowledge Moves beyond Human Understanding
affiliations: and Utah State University

detail.title: The Human-Machine Knowledge Gap: When Knowledge Moves beyond Human Understanding
detail.abstract: Throughout history, humans have relied on knowledge they cannot personally understand or verify. In most cases, however, that knowledge has remained somewhere within the collective human knowledge system. For example, one person may not understand a scientific theory, mathematical proof, or technical process, but other humans can. Artificial intelligence may fundamentally change this relationship. As AI becomes increasingly capable of generating discoveries, predictions, designs, proofs, and other forms of knowledge, society may eventually be able to validate and use knowledge that humans could not independently derive on their own. This paper introduces The Human-Machine Knowledge Gap (HMKG) to explain this possibility. HMKG argues that a human-machine knowledge gap develops when the knowledge society can use moves beyond the knowledge humans can independently derive. The theory distinguishes between the Human Knowledge Frontier, the Machine Knowledge Frontier, and the Usable Knowledge Frontier. It further distinguishes between the Knowledge Breadth Gap, which reflects how much usable knowledge lies beyond independent human derivation, and the Knowledge Depth Gap, which reflects how deeply current knowledge depends on earlier layers of machine-generated knowledge. The theory also introduces knowledge inheritance and the cost of human knowledge independence to explain how this gap can become self-reinforcing. The central argument is simple: society may continue to become more knowledgeable and more capable even while humans become increasingly unable to independently derive the knowledge on which that progress depends.

title: Band-owned Iso-budget Computation for Native Character-identity Streams
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Band-owned Iso-budget Computation for Native Character-identity Streams
detail.abstract: The NINMENI research program fixes identity granularity as a premise: one normalised character is one NMU identity, one ordered stream position, and one prediction target. The resulting long identity streams make computational form, rather than identity compression, the engineering variable. This paper reports MULTIPITA, a sequence of three implementations developed to distribute that work without merging, skipping, or pooling identities. MP0 organised eight fast and eight slow temporal ranges but retained a full dense cell for every character. MP1 corrected the slow path by projecting each completed window once before broadcasting it, reducing projection rows by 252.06× at the production piece shape while preserving complete output, state, and gradient oracles. The dominant dense cell nevertheless remained unchanged. MP2 replaces that cell with eight 96-channel fast blocks and assigns the exact removed parameter budget to eight boundary-owned slow banks. For model width 768, both MP0 and MP2 contain 7,077,888 cell parameters per layer; the complete candidate remains 98,127,393 parameters. The preregistered arithmetic gives a 7.7879× reduction in amortised cell MACs and a 4.7072× reduction in the counted linear work per production piece. On an RTX 4060, an isolated one-layer B = 8, T = 2048 harness measures 3.1907× faster forward and 2.1112× faster forward-plus-backward linear operators. These are not end-to-end speedups. A samerevision cold trainer control measured MP0 at 241.583 seconds per optimizer step and MP2 at 242.839 seconds, showing that the initial MP2 port alone did not remove the dominant full-stack bottleneck. After separate exact-stack changes to Emylton execution, precision, state handling, and synchronization, the active MP2 stack measured 21.258 seconds per step at 131,072 characters per optimizer step. That later result cannot be causally attributed to MP2 alone. A completed 500-step pilot records finite loss and gradients in every row, no row with zero positive crystal mass, and a median of 21 seconds between pretraining rows. We claim preservation of the native identity contract, exact parameter budget, mechanical conformance, and measured systems costs. We make no claim that MP2 preserves or improves learned model quality; the required matched trained comparison does not yet exist.

title: Competition through Storage
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business, University of Bergamo - Department of Economics and University of Bergamo

detail.title: Competition through Storage
detail.abstract: We study a conglomerate merger across different markets for storable goods where intermediaries (or consumers) carry inventories over time. A price change in one market reallocates inventories across otherwise independent markets. The resulting intertemporal cross-market externalities generate competition through storage. The merged multiproduct firm cuts prices whenever profit margins are expected to rise, because inventories cannibalize more profitable future sales, but raises prices whenever margins are expected to fall, because inventories shift sales toward the high-margin period. Profit margins are expected to rise in expanding markets, but to fall in mature markets with cost inflation if and only if cost pass-through is incomplete. Our analysis provides a practical screen for conglomerate merger assessment based on demand dynamics, cost dynamics, and cost pass-through.

title:
From "Disorder," "Suffering," "Artifice," and "Obscuration" to "Death": 
An Etiological Diagnosis of the Human Predicament
A Comparative Philosophical Study of Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism, Wang Yangming's School of Mind, and Calvinism

detail.title:
From "Disorder," "Suffering," "Artifice," and "Obscuration" to "Death": 
An Etiological Diagnosis of the Human Predicament
A Comparative Philosophical Study of Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism, Wang Yangming's School of Mind, and Calvinism
detail.abstract: This paper develops a new comparative framework for five traditions-Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism, Wang Yangming's School of Mind, and Calvinism (Reformed theology)-that does not begin by ranking their respective "therapies," but instead asks a more fundamental question: do these five traditions, in fact, diagnose the same underlying human problem? To this end, the paper develops a tripartite "Diagnosis-Etiology-Therapy" model and four criteria of "diagnostic adequacy" (phenomenological, causal, integrative, and therapeutic adequacy), applying them to examine the internal coherence of five diagnoses: the Confucian "disorder" (luan), the Buddhist "suffering" (ku), the Daoist "artifice" (wei), Yangming's "obscuration" (bi), and the Reformed "death." Building on this analysis, the paper distinguishes "descriptive comparison" from "reconstructive comparison," and, writing explicitly from a Reformed theological standpoint, advances a reconstructive, falsifiable hypothesis: that disorder, suffering, artifice, and obscuration may be understood as four phenomenological manifestations of "spiritual death" across the social, existential, natural, and moral domains. The paper further identifies a shared * Wenfu Zheng holds an MDiv from Lancaster Bible College (2021), a ThM from Puritan Reformed Theological Seminary (2024), and a PhD from Xi'an Jiaotong University (1998). He is currently a planting pastor at the Chinese Reformed Baptist Church at West Houston.

title: The Role of Social Media in Enhancing Awareness of Sustainable Development Goals Among Arab Youth
affiliations: , Al Ain University, Al Ain University and Al Ain University of Science & Technology - College of Business

detail.title: The Role of Social Media in Enhancing Awareness of Sustainable Development Goals Among Arab Youth
detail.abstract: Social media has become a central arena for informal learning and civic participation, yet its capacity to convert exposure into meaningful sustainability engagement remains uncertain. This study examines the role of social media in enhancing awareness of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) among Arab youth and explores how digital platforms function as spaces for informal learning. A cross-sectional quantitative survey was administered to 370 respondents aged 17–45 across several Arab countries (primarily the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria—countries selected because they are among the region’s most digitally connected societies and jointly represent the Gulf, Levantine, and North African sub-regions), measuring social media usage patterns, levels of SDG awareness, and forms of digital engagement; the data were analysed using descriptive statistics and inferential statistics (Pearson correlations, t-tests, and one-way ANOVA) that tested four hypotheses derived from an integrated research model. The findings show that visually oriented platforms, particularly Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok, dominate youth media consumption, and that social media is the leading source of SDG-related information for the majority of respondents. However, engagement remains largely passive, confined to viewing, liking, and resharing content, revealing a persistent gap between awareness and active participation. The hypothesis tests confirm this pattern: SDG awareness is strongly associated with digital engagement (r = 0.71, p < 0.001), whereas breadth of platform use plays only a marginal role (r = 0.11, p = 0.044) and membership in sustainability-focused online groups confers no significant awareness advantage. Drawing on Uses and Gratifications Theory and Knowledge Management Theory, the study introduces the Digital Awareness–Engagement Conversion Model (DAECM), which conceptualizes the staged transition from digital exposure to engagement and advocacy. The results underline the need for interactive, localised, and youth-centred digital strategies that can translate passive awareness into sustained sustainability action. Given the non-probability sampling design, the findings are interpreted as exploratory.

detail.abstract: Decision models typically treat choices as self-contained episodes and therefore do not explain how unresolved valuation, constraint, influence, justification, or authorship conditions generated through expression shape later decisions. This paper develops Cognitive Residue Decision Selection (CRDS), a cross-cycle extension of Conflict-Penalized Decision Selection (CPDS). CRDS specifies a five-stage account. First, it establishes whether expression leaves an unresolved trace and classifies the trace and its routing from longitudinal evidence. Second, PRM compares candidate changes in weights, valuations, conflict sensitivity, conflict costs, or authorship conditions. Third, CRDS tests whether the resulting state improves prediction beyond baseline CPDS. Finally, Lifecycle Coherence evaluates the connected trajectory by tracking authorship continuity, structural alignment, and normalized conflict across repeated cycles. Six propositions test the model's principal implications: changes in later selection under retained or propagated residue, persistence of burden, authorship-conditioned avoidance, CDD-induced False Repair, escalation under undischarged recurrence, and removal of trace-specific divergence after discharge. CRDS is a theoretical model that defines a broader empirical research program; it is not a validated diagnostic protocol. Evaluation requires comparable longitudinal cycles, reliable residue-routing coding, prespecified PRM comparisons, sensitivity analysis, and predictive validation against baseline CPDS and competing explanations.

title: A Funding-Flow Portfolio Optimisation Framework for Early-Stage Venture Capital in India: Evidence from Seven Startup Sectors, 2019–2025

detail.abstract: Analyzing Indian early-stage venture capital flows presents substantial challenges because funding activity varies considerably across sectors and over time. Between 2019 and 2025, capital has shifted wildly across seven key sectors: Consumer Services, Fintech, Ecommerce, Enterprise SaaS, AI/ML, Healthtech, and Edtech. To make sense of these movements, we built and validated a custom portfolio optimization framework designed specifically for these volatile capital flows. Six years of data for seven sectors creates an immediate statistical roadblock: Estimating a 7×7 covariance matrix from just six annual observations results in rank-deficiency, a well-known small-sample estimation problem. To separate signal from noise, we applied Ledoit–Wolf covariance shrinkage (Ledoit and Wolf 2004) (α = 0. 2505) to obtain a more stable covariance estimator, performed eigenvalue decomposition on the corrected matrix to expose latent market structures, and derived the Survival-Adjusted Blend (SAB). Rather than naively chasing yield, SAB tempers pure return optimization by weaving in actual sector-level startup mortality rates. A crucial distinction must be drawn up front: our dependent variable measures log funding-flow growth, not realized investment returns. Every metric reported acts as a Funding-Flow Attractiveness Proxy (FFAP) a measure of sector-level funding momentum efficiency, not cash returned to limited partners. Once cleaned, the data revealed a striking pattern. The primary macro capital factor (PC1) drives 61.5% of cross-sector variance (95% CI: [36.7%, 93.8%]). This factor correlates moderately ( 𝑟 =+ 0. 418) with inverted US Federal Reserve rate changes, mirroring the direct reach of global liquidity tides into Indian startup funding. To assess SAB robustness, we implement leave-one-out cross-validation against six competing strategies, reporting all results including periods of underperformance. Leave-one-out cross-validation showed SAB outperforming an equal-weight baseline in 4 of 6 held-out periods and beating a momentum strategy in 5 of 6. However, an unconstrained Maximum Sharpe model beat SAB in 4 of 6 periods a limitation we openly report. When pitted against six alternative strategies (equal weight, minimum variance, maximum Sharpe, inverse volatility, momentum, and a naive AI overweight), SAB ranks third on FFAP Sharpe (0.384 versus Max Sharpe's 0.484). Max Sharpe achieves this by concentrating 75% of capital in a single sector. For most funds, such concentration is operationally infeasible given LP mandate constraints and deal-flow limitations. SAB offers a sensible, realistic middle ground. Finally, when we audited the estimated dollar-weighted allocations of five leading Indian VC funds against our framework, the real-world gap was obvious. Across non-Kalaari funds, we documented a persistent overweighting of Ecommerce and a heavy underweighting of AI/ML falling short of SAB’s benchmark by 22 to 53 percentage points. We explicitly retract any claim that SAB "outperforms" these funds in terms of actual cash-on-cash investment returns. To be entirely transparent: we make no claim of delivering superior financial ROI. What our analysis actually demonstrates is that SAB generates distinctly higher model-implied, sector-level funding momentum efficiency (FFAP) than the estimated capital allocations of real-world funds.

detail.abstract: Many higher education institutions seek to use artificial intelligence for educational analytics but lack the infrastructure, expertise, or resources required to train, fine-tune, or host large language models locally. This study proposes an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-as-a-Service (AIaaS) score-stacking framework for Vietnamese student feedback sentiment analysis. Instead of treating Large Language Models (LLMs) as direct label predictors, the framework uses externally served LLMs as continuous sentiment scorers. Gemma-4-31B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instant, and Qwen3-32B were accessed through AIaaS inference platforms to assign sentiment scores in the interval [-1, 1] to 16,169 sentences from the University of Information Technology-Vietnamese Students' Feedback Corpus (UIT-VSFC) corpus. These scores were transformed into raw-score, aggregate, disagreement, and interaction features, then used to train lightweight local decision models. The novelty of this approach lies in using externally served LLM outputs as continuous meta-learning signals rather than as final sentiment labels. The evaluation compared fixedthreshold baselines, tuned-threshold baselines, equal and weighted score aggregation, and probability-stacking classifiers. In this evaluation, probability-stacking models achieved higher macro-F1 than direct thresholding and simple score aggregation. The final model, ExtraTrees stacking with probability-bias tuning selected by development-set macro-F1, achieved a test macro-F1 of 0.790. The findings suggest that, in this setting, the value of multi-model AIaaS lies not in naive averaging but in locally calibrated decision learning over continuous LLM score signals. This study contributes a technically feasible and auditable architecture for lowinfrastructure higher education analytics, where institutions can exploit external LLM capabilities while retaining local control over calibration, evaluation, and decision-making.

detail.abstract: What customer problems do entrepreneurs attempt to solve, and what determines which problems attract effort and capital? We construct the first large-scale database of the problems the startup economy addresses, using large language models to write a solution-agnostic problem statement for each of roughly 90,000 VC-backed U.S. startups, validating them against 331 founder interviews, and clustering them into a taxonomy of 265 problems. Six facts emerge. First, each problem is addressed by many distinct technologies and draws firms from several industries. Second, most technologies are narrow; a few, artificial intelligence among them, span nearly the entire problem space. Third, two-thirds of problems reflect enduring human and organizational needs rather than transient technological, regulatory, or social triggers. Fourth, capital concentrates far more sharply than entry: the ten largest clusters absorb one-third of aggregate venture capital. Fifth, founders sort into problems that benefit from their own expertise. Sixth, ventures with such founder-problem fit raise significantly more capital. The direction of entrepreneurship thus depends on who becomes a founder and how capital is allocated, not only on what the technological frontier makes possible.

title: Drawing Borders, Losing Talent: Geopolitical Risk and Workforce Reallocation
affiliations: , Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: Drawing Borders, Losing Talent: Geopolitical Risk and Workforce Reallocation
detail.abstract: Geopolitical risk challenges global production networks not only by disrupting trade and capital allocation but also by reshaping labor, a productive input that firms do not own and cannot redeploy unilaterally. We study how bilateral geopolitical tensions between multinational enterprises' (MNEs') home and host countries affect workforce reallocation across global firm networks. A sequential firm-worker model predicts that rising bilateral risk increases net labor outflow from exposed subsidiaries to other firms in the host country. Using a bilateral geopolitical risk index constructed from GDELT 2.0 conflict events and worker-level employment histories for 19,626 MNEs across 61 host countries over 2015-2025, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in bilateral risk raises net labor outflow by 0.47 workers per 100 employees per year. Approximately 77 percent of this net response is absorbed by other employers in the same host country, whereas intrafirm transfers to headquarters show no response. Difference-indifferences designs around major geopolitical shocks (e.g., the 2022 Russia-Ukraine War and the 2018 China-U.S. trade war) yield the same laborflow pattern.Mechanism tests rule out destination wage premia, rival-firm recruiting expansion, strategic MNE layoffs, and cross-border mobility frictions as explanations. Instead, workers tend to remain in the host country and join locally headquartered employers while preserving their occupations and industries, consistent with worker-driven safety-and stability-seeking. The resulting labor outflows are associated with less effective, less generous, and less transparent hiring, as well as weaker subsequent innovation at the MNE. At the aggregate global-network level, employment in high-GPR host countries declines while employment in moderate-GPR host countries rises, with no evidence of employment expansion at headquarters. These findings reveal a structural limit to reshoring and friendshoring: under geopolitical risk, labor does not move like capital and often does not come home.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly participates in the processes through which institutions interpret information, evaluate evidence, generate recommendations, make decisions, and act. Existing research and governance frameworks address AI risk management, human oversight, appropriate reliance, accountability, decision governance, and increasingly autonomous systems. A broader question nevertheless arises: how should institutions govern consequential judgment when the capabilities contributing to decisions and actions are distributed across human and artificial participants? This article advances Institutional Judgment Governance (IJG) as an integrative theoretical framework for examining that problem. IJG is defined as the governance of how institutions form, exercise, distribute, authorize, and evaluate consequential judgment; preserve the capacities required for such judgment; and remain accountable when human and artificial capabilities jointly contribute to organizational decision-making and action. It treats consequential institutional judgment as an institutionally attributable object of governance connecting AI capability with reliance, decision authority, delegated authority, judgment capacity, organizational action, and continuing accountability. The article makes four principal contributions. First, it distinguishes the exercise of institutional judgment from the institution’s continuing judgment capacity. Second, it distinguishes human presence, human oversight, human decision authority, and meaningful human judgment. Third, it identifies a two-sided governance problem: institutions must govern both the decision weight artificial contributions are permitted to carry and the institutional judgment capacity required to evaluate, challenge, and remain accountable for the resulting judgment. Fourth, it organizes the framework through six propositions: Institutional Accountability, Reliance Authorization, Effective Human Decision Authority, Judgment Preservation, Governed Delegation, and Reassessment and Adaptation. IJG complements rather than replaces established approaches to AI risk management, oversight, assurance, decision governance, evidentiary control, and authority allocation. Within IJG, Reliance Authorization is positioned as one governance model for structuring the institutional determination of whether, when, by whose authority, and under what conditions an AI contribution may carry consequential institutional decision weight. IJG’s proposed contribution is therefore configurational and integrative: it treats consequential institutional judgment as the integrative governance object around which Reliance Authorization, decision authority, institutional judgment capacity, accountability, and continuing reassessment are analyzed together.

detail.abstract: Post-trade operational systems-recording trades, positions, settlement states, fails, financing, and inventory-contain a rich record of institutional behaviour that is overwhelmingly used for operational purposes only. This paper presents a quantitative framework for estimating the forward post-trade state: where the institutional balance sheet is contractually and behaviourally heading, before all settlement has completed. We formalize a point-in-time state representation, decompose the post-trade state into marketaligned and residual components via a common-factor mapping, model settlement fail propagation using self-exciting Hawkes processes and graph theory, and formulate falsifiable hypotheses about whether these components contain incremental predictive information beyond contemporaneous market data. The framework is explicitly designed as a methodology and research agenda rather than an empirical findings paper. All numerical examples, model parameters, figures, and outputs are simulated and are included solely to illustrate the proposed methodology. The mathematical architecture is designed so that quantitative models produce all numerical estimates, while AI assists in interpretation and communication rather than calculation.

detail.abstract:
Distributed ledgers commonly place irreversible history under one dominant control resource: computation, stake, configured validator authority, or an operator-controlled ordering service. Hybrid protocols may diversify resources while permitting them to compensate for one another in an aggregate score. This paper develops a different architecture: asymmetric non-substitutable finality (ANSF). One independently constituted domain pre-locks the prior-final history and a transaction-availability commitment; a second domain executes the committed input and supplies economic or institutional accountability; and a separately sampled closing function verifies correspondence between the committed input, resulting state, and prior lock. Finality exists only when all typed certificates match. Excess stake, work, signatures, or institutional authority in one domain cannot replace a missing certificate from another.

Therefore, the architecture converts safety failure from capture of one resource into a
conditional intersection of failures across required domains. Its cost is equally important:
liveness failure becomes a union, because any required domain can pause full finality.
Three refinements address the dominant practical risks in the basic formulation. First, a
graduated finality policy allows different transaction classes to require different subsets of
domains, so that the liveness tax is not uniform while the non-substitution core is
preserved for high-value irreversible settlement. Second, domain independence is treated
as a continuously evaluated residual-risk predicate rather than a binary assumption; the
probability of full safety failure is bounded by the intersection of domain failures plus the
residual common-mode term. Third, the non-bypass recovery rule and the formal kernel
are strengthened so that reconstitution remains strictly prospective and no single domain
can manufacture a missing certificate.

The paper corrects an intuitive but erroneous two-thirds attack claim, distinguishes
certificate formation from conflicting-quorum safety, models random personhood-derived
committees, and shows why common software, infrastructure, credential, and
jurisdictional dependencies can dominate apparently spectacular committee probabilities.
The paper grounds the architecture in the 2024-2026 record: it positions ANSF against the
fast-finality and asymmetric-trust research lines, adds a documented common-mode case
study, anchors the institutional application in live tokenized-settlement programmes, maps
the graduated finality classes onto legal settlement-finality frameworks, and quantifies the
post-quantum cost argument. The proposal remains a research architecture, not a
completed consensus proof. Its value lies in a precise program for formal verification,
adversarial simulation with correlated failures, and institutional experimentation in
tokenized settlement systems where no single constituency should determine irreversible
history.

title: Macroeconomic Distortions and Economic Growth: Analysis of Income and Temporal Heterogeneity
affiliations: Western Washington University - College of Business & Economics and

detail.title: Macroeconomic Distortions and Economic Growth: Analysis of Income and Temporal Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: This paper examines how macroeconomic policy distortions shape economic growth using a global panel spanning 1961-2022. Combining standard macroeconomic indicators with subcomponents of the Economic Freedom of the World (EFW) index, we estimate fixed effects and system GMM models to address unobserved heterogeneity and endogeneity. We document substantial heterogeneity in the growth effects of distortions across income groups and time. The black market premium emerges as a robust and pervasive drag on growth across all specifications. In contrast, the effects of inflation and trade distortions are conditional on both the income level and the period. Notably, in the post-1999 sample, under-trading becomes a significant and broadly shared constraint on growth across all income cohorts. These findings indicate that the growth consequences of policy distortions are neither uniform nor stable over time, underscoring the importance of context-specific and income-sensitive policy design rather than onesize-fits-all reform strategies.

title: Diagonal Frog Meets ADI: Trading Matrix Exponentials for Rational Maps in the Fokker-Planck Equation
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - NYU Tandon School of Engineering and

detail.title: Diagonal Frog Meets ADI: Trading Matrix Exponentials for Rational Maps in the Fokker-Planck Equation

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received.

detail.abstract: A companion paper [Itkin, 2026a] introduced the Diagonal Frog (DF) positivity-preserving schemes for anisotropic Fokker-Planck equations, advancing each directional substep by a Krylov-computed matrix exponential, which dominates the cost. Replacing that exponential by a rational map r(γL) reduces the substep to a banded solve, but the positivity argument no longer applies. We prove that for eventually exponentially positive generators the entrywise sign of r(γL) at large steps is decided by a single number, the value r(∞) taken on infinitely stiff modes. Nonnegativity holds above a computable threshold when 0 ≤ r(∞) < 1, and at most on a bounded interval, empty or vanishingly narrow in all our tests, when r(∞) < 0. The criterion rejects the Crank-Nicolson (trapezoidal) method, where r(∞) =-1, and selects the subdiagonal Padé(0, 2) method, which is second order, L-stable and provably positive above an explicit threshold. The resulting DF-ADI scheme costs O(N) per step, keeps the implicit factorized mixed derivative unchanged, is second order in space and time, and conserves discrete mass exactly. In the strong cross-diffusion regime, however, the directional factors demand a step larger than the mixed derivative permits, so the composite second-order scheme is only empirically positive there, and the criterion serves to discriminate the well-behaved multiplicative factors from the stabilizing-correction schemes rather than to guarantee positivity. Against the Krylov exponential it runs ten to thirty-two times faster at matched accuracy in our tests with the gain growing with the mesh. We extend the construction to the backward Kolmogorov equation and to jump-diffusion models.

title: Deflation and Financial Stress in the Great Recession
affiliations: The University of Austin

detail.title: Deflation and Financial Stress in the Great Recession
detail.abstract: In the Great Recession of 2007-2009, the US economy experienced deflation and a concurrent financial crisis. Did tight money cause a credit crunch, or did the credit contraction cause monetary tightness? I test for Granger causality between monetary tightness implied by Treasury Inflation Protected Securities (TIPS) and financial stress indicated by the Treasury-Eurodollar (TED) spread and the St. Louis Fed's Financial Stress Index. Prior to the crisis, changes in inflation Granger cause changes in financial stress, but changes in financial stress do not Granger cause changes in inflation, providing preliminary evidence that tight money may have triggered the financial crisis.
